# Progress and issue log

Newest first. Each entry: date, what changed, evidence, open issues.

## 2026-11-04 — One Outlook failure, one line, one dismiss

The job strip rendered every failed job as its own line and its own action.
Repeated Outlook reconnects and discovery failures piled up as many "Fermer
Outlook" buttons, and each line carried the raw Go wrapper chain
("syncer: details of outlook: outlook: ..."). The action label also read as an
instruction to close Outlook itself.

The fix is at the two owners, not in the copy.

**Server.** `jobs.Info` now carries `cause`, the stable translatable identity of
a source precondition. The manager reads it through a small structural
interface, so `internal/jobs` does not import the source package. The Outlook
unavailability errors already exposed the code; the unexported type now also
has a `Cause()` method for callers that only know the interface.

**Console.** `jobGroups` folds failed jobs with the same producer and cause into
one incident, keeps the newest attempt as the representative, and shows the
attempt count. `jobCauseText` translates `api.source_cause.<code>` and falls
back to the bounded redacted diagnostic only when the producer named no cause.
`paintJobActions` emits one action per incident; dismissing it removes every job
in the group. The visible button is one short verb, while the accessible label
and title still name the job. French now says "Masquer l'avis" and "Annuler la
tâche" instead of "Fermer Outlook" and "Annuler Classifieur local".

**Evidence.** `go test ./internal/jobs ./internal/source ./internal/ui
./internal/api` passes. The new manager test finds the cause through a wrapped
error and proves a plain failure has no cause. The new Node harness proves three
warming-up failures become one group with the newest representative and a
translated cause, while an unknown cause keeps its bounded diagnostic. The
Playwright live and resilience specs pass (16 tests). `scripts/test-fast.sh`
exits 0; the exhaustive gate result is recorded after it completes.

**Residual risk.** A producer that has no stable cause still shows its redacted
diagnostic. The group key includes the cause, so two different causes for the
same producer remain two incidents, which is intended.


## 2026-11-04 — CI round: first paint, dependency and analysis

The first CI run found three causes, not 157 separate UI bugs.

**Playwright.** The shared E2E server booted a fresh data directory with the
setup marker unset, so the first-run overlay hid `#app` and every spec timed out
on it. The shared server now sets `MAILSENSE_UI_SETUP_DONE=true`. A dedicated
`e2e/specs/setup.spec.ts` starts its own server with the variable **unset**, not
false: an env override outranks the file layer, so `false` made the marker
impossible to persist. The spec drives the overlay in English, saves French,
skips the mail step, finishes, and proves a reload does not reopen it. The full
suite passes: 180 tests.

**Vulnerability scan.** `govulncheck` found GO-2026-6860 reachable through
`golang.org/x/net@v0.61.0` in `internal/render`. Upgraded to `v0.62.0` and
declared `go 1.27.3` in `go.mod` so the standard-library fixes in 1.27.2 and
1.27.3 are in scope. `govulncheck ./...` now reports no vulnerabilities.

**CodeQL.** Nineteen alerts came from provider secret **names** embedded in
error text and then logged. The three error owners no longer include the name:
the provider id and "no usable key" are enough. Two `int64` to `int` narrowing
sites now have explicit bounds (`body_chars`, `prior_min_samples`, embedding
index). The repository's default CodeQL setup was disabled because the advanced
workflow already analyzes both Go and JavaScript; two analyses of the same PR
produced a duplicate failing check.

**Evidence.** Full Playwright suite 180 passed. `govulncheck ./...` reports no
vulnerabilities. The final fast and exhaustive runs on this tree are recorded
below in this entry once they complete.

**Residual risk.** CodeQL's path-injection query flags the deliberate `fsx` and
`digest` filesystem choke points, and its SSRF query flags the user-configured
provider base URL. Both are design constraints, not exploitable paths for a
local desktop app, but they remain visible as code-scanning alerts. The setup
overlay still has no full focus trap.


## 2026-11-04 — First run, honest docs, and a clean public tree

The release round closed three gaps at once.

**First run.** `ui.setup.done` is in the schema, `GET /api/setup` projects the
state, and `internal/ui/js/05-setup.js` is an overlay with welcome (data
directory, discovered stores, language, zone), mail, model and finish steps. It
writes the ordinary settings route and reuses the mailbox, zone, language and
provider routes. The completion predicate keys off a **selected** mailbox, not a
discovered one: startup discovery pre-fetches store rows, so counting them would
keep the wizard closed on a fresh Windows install. The regression test uses two
discovered, unselected stores. A Not now action makes the mail step escapable,
and a language choice is applied before the next step paints.

**Docs.** The install, first-run, privacy and troubleshooting pages now match
the product: classic Outlook COM on Windows, no Microsoft sign-in, Linux preview
with no live source, a runtime downloaded on first use (342 MB Windows, 328 MB
Linux), no SQL console, no diagnostics export, local training, automatic triage
requests, and a setup screen that exists. Six bilingual guide pairs were added
(mailboxes, providers, learning, FAQ, security, contributing). `docs/SELLING.md`
was rewritten around the same limits. The public page list is declared once in
`internal/site` and the release tarball reads it.

**PII.** The invented cast is consistent across labels, addresses and query
terms. Residue in `internal/qa` and `internal/store` comments, addresses and
fixtures was fixed, and the ten stale `internal/qa` tests from the rename were
realigned to the cast. The contract greps for old business stems, real person
names, machine paths and internal vendors all return zero.

**Evidence.** `scripts/test-fast.sh` exit 0 and `scripts/test.sh` exit 0 on the
final tree. `go test` passes for `internal/qa`, `internal/store`,
`internal/contacts`, `internal/mail`, `internal/world`, `internal/conversations`,
`internal/engine`, `internal/api`, `internal/ui`, `internal/prose` and
`internal/site`. `make site-check` reports the generated surface current. The
setup contract tests cover the overlay manifest, boot order, route reuse and
catalog coverage; the API tests cover a fresh install, a marker, a selected
mailbox, discovered-but-unselected stores, and the marker write through the
settings route.

**Residual risk.** The overlay has no full focus trap. Windows and WebView2 first
paint remain unverified on this Linux host. The two keys deleted from `.env` are
still valid until the owner revokes them.


## 2026-11-04 — One owner for the enforced setting keys

The store audit's fourteenth finding: the store and the search path read eleven
configuration keys as literals — `store.max_open_conns`, four `query.*` bounds
and six `search.*` limits — so a key had to be typed identically in two packages
and a ceiling could be raised in one reader and misspelled in the other.

`store/settings.go` now declares one constant per key (the store is the lower
package; `internal/search` already imports it). The store's open, read-only pool
and search entry read them, and `internal/search` reads the same names for the
limit, character budget, embedding timeout, RRF constant and snippet size.

**Regression.** `TestSettingKeysHaveOneOwner` requires each key literal to
appear exactly once across both packages, in `settings.go`, and pins each
reader's use of the constant.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a reader typing the key again
(`setting "store.max_open_conns" is spelled 2 times`); the ceiling key no longer
matching the schema (`TestFilterSetExtendsWithNewMail` fails in
`internal/search`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store ./internal/search`; both suites pass
(21.8 s and 8.3 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (95 s).

**Residual risk.** The search-only keys (`search.limit`, `search.rrf_k`,
`snippet_chars`, `embed_timeout`, `query_max_chars`) live in `store` because it
is the common package; a future package that needs them without importing the
store would justify a neutral settings-key owner, and the guard would point at
it. The keys still come from the schema; the constants name them, they do not
set defaults. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One JSON-set membership subquery

The store audit's eleventh finding: `IN (SELECT value FROM json_each(?))` was
written out at thirteen sites across nine files — address scope, the company
book, company evidence bodies, conversation participants, people, search, thread
states, the triage decision scope and four world reads — beside `idSetSQL`,
which already owned the same subquery for row ids. A change to the membership
shape would have reached only the id set.

`stringSetSQL` now aliases `idSetSQL` in `lists.go`, so the subquery is written
once and the two names document which value type the caller binds. All thirteen
sites read it; none spells the subquery.

**Regression.** `TestStringSetSQLHasOneOwner` scans every non-test file: the
subquery appears once, only in `lists.go`; no second `stringSetSQL` literal
exists; and all nine consumers reference the shared name.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the alias re-spelled as its own literal
(`lists.go declares a second string-set literal`); the alias binding an empty
set (`TestCompanyBookTreatsMultiCompanyDomainAsShared` and three other company
reads fail, proving the shared name is the one the reads execute).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store`; `go test ./internal/store` passes
(56.5 s under load); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed
(374 s under load). One gate attempt failed on a full disk, not on code: the
host's root filesystem was at 100 % from another job, so `go clean -cache` and
the removal of the Playwright report directories were run and the gate rerun.

**Residual risk.** `stringSetSQL` and `idSetSQL` are the same text today; the two
names exist so a read can say which JSON type it binds, not to allow the shapes
to diverge. A future read that needs a different subquery (an `EXISTS`, a
typed cast) should add a named constant rather than edit this one. The stored
JSON lists are built by `jsonList` and `idSet`, which remain the one encoders.
The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One diagnostic disclosure component

The UI audit's second finding: the English diagnostic disclosure was hand-built
in seven modules with the same `details.blocker-diagnostic > summary + p`
markup, differing by summary key, paragraph class and one missing language
attribute (the Sources backfill). A technical block therefore read differently
depending on which screen showed it.

`diagnosticDetails(text, { summary, paragraphClass, dataset })` in
`01-components.js` now owns it: `details` with `lang="en"`, a summary key
(default `common.diagnostic`) and one English paragraph. The toast, the Ask
failure, the Sources backfill, the Labels blocker, the Search notice and the
error screen call it; `problemDiagnostic` delegates to it. One module now
contains the markup.

**Regressions.** `TestDiagnosticDetailsHasOneOwner` scans every UI module,
requires exactly one `blocker-diagnostic` occurrence (in the component) and
pins each caller's options. `TestJobProseStaysDiagnostic` was updated to follow
the owner: the Sources backfill is checked through `diagnosticDetails` and the
component is checked for the English stamp.

Mutation: a hand-built disclosure returning in `52-init.js` (the guard's module
scan) — recorded below.

**Evidence.** `go generate ./internal/ui`; `go test ./internal/ui` passes
(12.4 s). The browser suite ran 178/179; the single failure
(`scoped-search › Companies keeps … across a cached Back`) is environmental:
the host load average was 91 on 12 cores from another user's benchmark, the
same spec fails identically on the pre-round tree and with round 94's UI
restored, and its 8 s attribute wait is what times out. It is re-run once the
host is quiet.

**Residual risk.** The component's `dataset` option exists only for the Sources
backfill's `[data-backfill-message]` update hook; a caller that needs another
hook extends the options rather than rebuilding the block. The paragraph class
option keeps the three call-site variants (`fine`, `fine mono`, none) that
existed before, so the visual result is unchanged. The deployed build predates
this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One retrieval-degradation classifier

The Q&A audit's third finding: the semantic leg's health was classified three
ways. `ask.go` mapped it through `retrievalProblemOf` (a string type) into one of
two sentinels; `topic.go` checked only `res.Semantic.TimedOut` and hardcoded the
timeout notice; `company.go` mapped nothing. The gap the comment forbade was
real: a partially covered vector index with hits produced no notice on the topic
lane, so a warming index looked like a complete answer.

`retrievalProblemOf(sem)` now returns the sentinel itself (`nil`,
`errSearchTimeout`, `errSearchWarming`), with a timeout winning over a partial
copy, and the string `retrievalProblem` type is gone. The freeform path returns
the sentinel directly; the topic lane maps any degradation through
`retrievalNotice`, so a timeout and a warming index reach their own notice and
reason and neither is hardcoded. `company.go` still returns its search error
unchanged and is called out below.

**Regressions.** `TestRetrievalProblemClassifiesTheSemanticLeg` covers a complete
index, no eligible mail, a partial copy, a timeout and a timeout on a partial
copy. `TestTopicDegradationReportsAPartialIndex` drives the topic lane with hits
and `Covered: 1, Eligible: 5` and requires `NoticeIndexWarming`.
`TestTopicNoticeComesFromTheOneMapping` refuses a hardcoded timeout notice in
`topic.go`, requires the shared classifier, pins one definition and refuses a
returning string type.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a timeout classified as warming
(`retrievalProblemOf = qa: semantic index is warming, want qa: retrieval timed
out`); the topic lane ignoring the semantic state (`topic notice = "", want
"qa_index_warming"`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/qa`; `go test ./internal/qa` passes (4.5 s); the
gate reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The topic lane now shows a notice where it used to answer from
whatever hits it had; that is the intended honesty fix, but it changes what a
partially indexed mailbox displays for a contact- or company-topic question. The
company-evidence search still propagates its error instead of degrading, because
a company answer has no notice slot yet; giving it one is a separate round.
`retrievalNotice` remains the single mapping from sentinel to notice and reason.
The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One summary vocabulary for the today path

The Q&A audit's second finding: `summaryVerbList` claimed to be "the one list of
summary verbs", and `entityStopwords` did derive from it, but the
`summary_today` intent kept its own literal list. The two had drifted:
`resumez`, `resumer`, `synthetise` and `recapitule` existed only in the verb list,
while `bilan`, `overview` and `brief` existed only in the intent list, so the
same spelling was a summary request on one path and a freeform question on the
other.

`summaryIntentWords` in `summary.go` now derives from `summaryVerbList` plus the
three summary nouns that are not verbs (`bilan`, `overview`, `brief`), and
`intentWords[IntentSummaryToday]` reads it. A new spelling reaches both paths.

**Regressions.** `TestSummaryIntentDerivesFromTheVerbList` refuses a literal
intent list, requires the derived reference, checks every verb and the three
nouns, and pins a sample of spellings. `TestSummaryIntentReachesEverySpelling`
drives `parseIntent` for five spellings and for a count question about another
week.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a pinned spelling removed from the verb
list (`summaryIntentWords lacks the pinned spelling "resumez"`); the literal
list put back in `intent.go` (`intent.go spells the summary-intent list
itself`). A first attempt removed `resumez` and stayed green because a today
question with a thread noun is summary today anyway, and the derivation test
iterates the list so it cannot see a removal; the pinned sample is what makes
the guard bite.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/qa`; `go test ./internal/qa` passes (4.4 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (150 s under load).

**Residual risk.** The today path now accepts every verb-list spelling, which is
the intended drift fix but widens what counts as a summary request: "résumez"
in a today question takes the deterministic summary path instead of freeform.
`bilan`, `overview` and `brief` stay intent-only nouns rather than entering the
verb list, so they do not become entity stopwords. The deployed build predates
this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One role-mailbox vocabulary

The Q&A audit's first finding: "a shared mailbox is not a person" had two
vocabularies. `entity.go` owned `mailboxWords` (with `rh`, `hr`, `facturation`,
`compta`, `direction`, `secretariat`, `commandes`) while `person.go` owned
`genericPersonTokens` (with `microsoft`, `google`, `apple`, `notifications`,
`accounts`), so "RH" was a role for entity linking and a person for a name
question, and "Support Team" and "Microsoft 365" were judged by different sets.

`internal/qa/rolewords.go` now declares `roleMailboxWords` once, as the union of
both lists, and every judge reads it: the display-name rule (`isPersonLike`), the
person-name guard (`personName`), the question-to-label match, and the company
contact desk selector. Both retired names are refused by the guard.

The union exposed a second rule that had been hiding behind the sets: mention
term extraction was dropping role words before the pool could decide, so the
question "services" no longer reached `dropGenericCandidates` and selected the
companies named "Info - Services …". Mention terms now keep every word and let
`genericEntityTerms` (computed from the candidate pool, never a phrase list)
drop a word shared by several organizations. `entityMention` keeps its other
static exclusions; only the role list moved out of it.

**Regressions.** `TestRoleMailboxVocabularyHasOneOwner` pins the single
definition, refuses both retired identifiers and requires the three consumers.
`TestRoleMailboxVocabularyCoversBothLists` pins the union and rejects ordinary
names. `TestRoleDisplayNamesAreNotPeople` covers RH Support, Microsoft 365,
Comptabilité Clients, two real names and a `personName` role hit. The existing
`TestGenericCompanyWordDoesNotSelectOrganizations` is what caught the extraction
regression during the round.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `rh`/`hr` removed from the union
(`roleMailboxWords lacks "rh"`); the display-name rule ignoring role words
(`isPersonLike("RH Support") = true, want false`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/qa`; `go test ./internal/qa` passes (1.8 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The union is wider than either list, so a company whose only
contact local part is `accounts@` or `notifications@` can now appear in a
company-contact answer where it did not before; that is the intended reading of
"role mailbox", but it is a user-visible change. Mention terms are now filtered
only by the pool and the static non-role exclusions, which is broader; the pool
rule plus the person-like filter is what keeps a role word from selecting an
identity. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One folders projection for a message

The store audit's seventeenth finding: the JSON subquery that reads a message's
further folders (`json_group_array(json_array(f2.path, f2.role))` over
`message_folders`) was spelled twice — once inside `itemsSQL` and once in
`detailBaseSQL` — with different indentation and no shared owner. A change to
the pair (a new column, an ordering rule) had to reach both reads.

`foldersSQL` in `items.go` now owns the projection. `itemsSQL` selects it after
the attachments array, and `detailBaseSQL` selects it after the detail columns;
both reads parse it through the same `parseItems` path.

**Regressions.** `TestFoldersProjectionHasOneOwner` pins one definition, one
spelling in `items.go`, none in `details.go`, and requires the detail read to
reference the owner. `TestFoldersReadAgreesBetweenItemsAndDetailBase` gives one
message a second folder and requires `readItems` and `loadDetailBases` to return
the same `[path, role]` pair.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the detail base re-spelling the subquery
(`details.go spells the folders projection itself`); the item read dropping the
parsed folders (`folders differ: items [], detail base []`, both reads empty
because they share the parser).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store`; `go test ./internal/store` passes
(16.4 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The projection assumes one row per (message, folder) pair and
orders by path; a message with two folders of the same path cannot exist under
the table's uniqueness. `parseItems` still treats a malformed folders value as a
decode error. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One FTS message reader and one id walker

The store audit's first finding: the full-text rebuilds read a message twice —
`reindexTri` and `reindexBatch` each carried the same six-column projection plus
the recipients parse — and both `reindexFull` and `reindexTri` repeated the same
keyset id scan (`SELECT id FROM messages WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?`).

`fts.go` now owns both:

- `readFTSMessage(ctx, q, id)` reads the one projection (`ftsMessageSQL`, which
  holds the only `recipientsSQL` reference in the file) and parses the
  recipients. Both writers call it, on the pool or inside the writer's
  transaction through `queryer`.
- `eachIDBatch(ctx, q, size, fn)` is the one keyset walker: ascending ids in
  batches of `sync.batch_size`, advancing past the last id of each batch. Both
  `reindexFull` and `reindexTri` walk through it.

**Regressions.** `TestFTSRebuildsShareOneReaderAndWalker` pins one definition of
each owner, one id-scan string, one recipients projection, both writers calling
the reader and both rebuilds calling the walker.
`TestFTSRebuildFindsEveryMessageInBatches` seeds five messages with a two-row
batch, clears the index and makes the text version stale, then requires the
reopen to index all five.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the word writer reading its own projection
again (`fts.go reads a message 1 times, want both writers`); the walker stopping
after one batch (`full rebuild indexed 2 messages, want 5`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store`; `go test ./internal/store` passes
(26.7 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The per-message read inside a batch is still one statement per
row; this round removes the duplicated statement, not the loop. A batched read
(`WHERE id IN idSetSQL`) would cut statements further but changes the trigram
pass's per-row clock accounting, so it needs its own round. The first version of
the behavior test passed under the mutation because the initial open had already
indexed the rows; the test now clears them, which is what made the mutation
visible. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One count check, panic error and paused log in the ranked views

The triage/priority audit's sixth finding: `Top`, `Actions` and `Decisions` each
built their own "count must be between 1 and 200" error, the two panic sites
each built their own `priority: … panicked (%T)`, and the paused-refresh log
line was written twice.

`countError(view, n)`, `panicError(what, value)` and `logRefreshPaused(err)` now
own those three rules in `view_errors.go`; the three views, the two recovery
paths and both pause branches call them. The helpers live in their own file
because `priority.go` was already at its reviewed line budget: the first attempt
at this round pushed it to 1568 lines and the structure ratchet refused it, so
the code was split by responsibility instead of raising the budget.

**Regression.** `TestRankedViewHelpersHaveOneOwner` pins one bound spelling, one
panic spelling and one paused-log spelling, requires the three view calls, and
checks the composed messages against the literal bound.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the shared bound widening
(`countError = "…and 201, got 0", want "…and 200, got 0"`); one panic error
re-spelled (`priority.go spells the panic error 2 times, want once`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/priority`; `go test ./internal/priority` passes
(1.9 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (75 s).

**Residual risk.** `countError` names the view with a short noun ("top",
"action", "decision"); a fourth view must pass its own noun rather than build a
message. The panic error keeps the value's type only, never its contents, so a
secret in a panic value cannot reach the log. `priority.go` is now 1550 lines
against its 1558 budget, ten lines of headroom. The deployed build predates this
change.

## 2026-11-04 — One spelling and one normalization for the ask vocabulary

The triage/priority audit's third finding: `action.AskAction` re-listed all seven
`asks_for` options while its own comment said `threadintel` owns the vocabulary,
and both it and `ClassifyAsk` normalized the value with their own
`strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(...))`.

`threadintel` now declares each option as a constant (`AskAnswerQuestion`,
`AskApprovalDecision`, `AskInformationDocument`, `AskPaymentMoney`,
`AskMeetingAvailability`, `AskTaskWork`, `AskNothingFYI`) and one `AskOption`
owns the normalization. `ClassifyAsk` switches on the constants;
`action.AskAction` reads `ClassifyAsk` for the structural cases (reply, FYI) and
`AskOption` plus the work constants for the owner-facing action.

**Regressions.** `TestAskActionReadsTheOneVocabulary` refuses any raw option in
`action.go`, requires the classification read, and covers all seven options plus
mixed case, spaces, unknown and empty.
`TestAskVocabularyIsDeclaredOnce` pins one declaration per option.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a raw literal in action
(`action.go spells "payment_money"`); the normalization dropping `TrimSpace`
(`AskAction("  Payment_Money ") = read, false; want pay, true`).

**Evidence.** `go vet`; `go test ./internal/action ./internal/threadintel`
passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The owner-facing primary (pay, schedule, send, do, decide) is
still a mapping in `action`, because it is the UI/ranking consequence rather
than the structural meaning; it now names the vocabulary by constant. A new
profile option needs a constant, a classification and, if it is concrete work,
a primary. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One clamp prologue for the world profile reads

The triage/priority audit's ninth finding: `world.Profile` and `world.Profiles`
each clamped the months and event-day windows with the same two `mathx.Clamp`
calls before building the cache key, so a bound change had to reach both or the
single and batch reads would key the same organization differently.

`profileWindow(months, eventDays)` now owns the clamp; both reads call it once
and use the returned values for the key and the build.

**Regression.** `TestProfileWindowHasOneOwner` pins one clamp per bound, two
call sites, the default values for `(0, -1)` and the maxima for values past the
bounds.

Mutation, failing as intended: the batch read clamping on its own again
(`world.go clamps months 2 times, want once in profileWindow`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/world`; `go test ./internal/world` passes
(3.4 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `profileWindowOf` takes and returns values rather than a
window type; if a third bound is added, the signature changes and both callers
follow. The cache key still encodes only the two windows, which is the store's
documented key. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One decider identity for the paid cache key

The triage/priority audit's third finding: the paid-cache identity of the
configured decider — provider id, model, fingerprint — was formatted in three
places in `triager.go`, while `engine.Provider.Key()` owned the same shape for
the provider record. A change to the shape could reach the record and not the
live decider.

`engine.DeciderKey(name, model, fingerprint)` now owns the string;
`Provider.Key()` delegates to it, and the three triage sites call it with the
live decider's parts.

**Regressions.** `TestDeciderKeyIsTheOneIdentity` pins the `a/b/c` shape and
requires `Provider.Key()` to equal the shared function for its own parts.
`TestDeciderKeyComesFromTheEngine` refuses a `Name() + "/"` expression in
`triager.go` and pins the three call sites.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the identity dropping the model
(`DeciderKey = "provider.example.test/fp-1", want "provider.example.test/deepseek-v4.1/fp-1"`);
triage re-spelling it (`triager.go re-spells the decider identity` and
`calls engine.DeciderKey 2 times, want three`).

**Evidence.** `go vet`; `go test ./internal/engine ./internal/triage` passes
(20.0 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The key is a plain concatenation with `/` separators; a
provider id or model containing `/` would be ambiguous, as it already was. The
function takes three strings rather than a `Decider` because `Provider` does not
implement the full `Decider` interface and both shapes must name the same key.
The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One cache identity for the triage page and summary

The triage/priority audit's third finding: `Page` and `Summary` each built the
`viewKey` that names their cached view, field by field, with the same mail and
route generations, preview flag, config version, fingerprint, route key and
decider. A field added to one and not the other would serve a page from the
summary's entry.

`cacheKey(ctx, id, limit, offset)` now builds the identity once; the page passes
its window and the summary passes the zero window. Both cache lookups read it.

**Regression.** `TestPageAndSummaryShareOneCacheKey` requires one `viewKey{`
literal in `page.go` (inside `cacheKey`) and both call sites, with the summary's
zero window.

Mutation, failing as intended: the summary building its own key again
(`page.go builds a viewKey 2 times, want once in cacheKey` and `lacks "key :=
t.cacheKey(ctx, id, 0, 0)"`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/triage`; `go test ./internal/triage` passes
(20.4 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The key is a struct, so a future field has one construction
site and the compiler forces both paths through it. `previewing(ctx)` is called
inside the helper, as before, so it still reads the live preview flag once per
request. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One owner for the triage decider setting

The triage/priority audit's second finding: `triage.decider` was a literal in
four places — three in `engines.go` and one in the `triager` cache key — which
the package's own setting-key contract forbids for every other key it stamps a
cache with. `layer1` also spelled it in five places and its tests in seven.

`DeciderSetting` now owns the key beside the other `triage.*` constants, and one
`errNoDecider()` builds the three identical "no triage decider is configured"
errors from it. Every read in `triage`, `layer1` and their tests uses the
constant; the contract test gained the row, so a new literal fails immediately.

**Regressions.** `TestSettingKeyLiteralsLiveOnlyInTheirOwner` now covers
`triage.decider` across `internal/triage`, `internal/judge` and `internal/layer1`
(including tests and build-tagged files). It caught the layer1 spellings this
round would otherwise have left behind.

Mutation, failing as intended: one layer1 call site spelling the literal again
(`../layer1/plan.go:79:24: "triage.decider" must be DeciderSetting`).

**Evidence.** `go vet`; `go test ./internal/triage` (18.9 s) and
`go test ./internal/layer1` (9.5 s) pass; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all
fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `layer1` already imports `triage`, so reading the constant
adds no dependency; a future package that must write `triage.decider` without
importing `triage` would need the key moved to a neutral owner, and the contract
would fail first. `errNoDecider` keeps the setting name in its message from the
constant, so the message cannot drift. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One reply flag and one decision predicate on the ranked row

The triage/priority audit's fourth and fifth findings. `Item` carried the reply
obligation twice — the exported `ReplyOpen` the wire reads and an unexported
`replyOpen` the Reply filter read — plus `isQuestion` and `callToAction`, which
nothing read at all. And the Decisions view rebuilt the decision predicate that
`Filter.matches` already owns.

`ReplyOpen` is now the only reply flag; the Reply filter reads it, and the three
unexported fields are gone (with their assignment in `signals.go`). `Decisions`
asks `FilterDecision.matches(r.item)` instead of comparing the action and its
waiting state itself.

**Regressions.** `TestDecisionsReadsTheOnePredicate` requires the Decisions body
to call the filter and refuses a second `action.Decide &&` expression or a
returning `replyOpen` field. `TestDecisionFilterMatchesOnlyTheOwnersPendingDecision`
covers an owner-facing decision, the other side's, nothing pending and a
non-decision. `TestFilters` still covers the Reply filter against the derived
flag.

Mutations, each failing as intended: Decisions building its own predicate
(`Decisions builds its own decision predicate`); the Reply filter reading
`ReplyNeeded` instead of the derived obligation (`reply: match false, want true`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/priority`; `go test ./internal/priority` passes
(2.4 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `isQuestion` and `callToAction` were removed because nothing
read the copies on the wire row; the row signals still carry the same facts for
the scorer. A future filter that needs them must read the signal, not add a
second item field. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One ask vocabulary for the reply obligation

The triage/priority audit's second finding: "the owner owes a reply" was stated
twice with incompatible operators. `priority.replyOwed` compared the raw ask
with `!= "nothing_fyi"` (case-sensitive), while `threadintel.asksOwner` used
`EqualFold(…, "answer_question")`. A profile value typed with different case
could open an obligation on one screen and not the other, and the asks_for
options were spelled in two packages.

Both rules now read `threadintel.ClassifyAsk`, the declared owner of the
vocabulary: `asksOwner` is `ReplyNeeded || ClassifyAsk(AsksFor) == AskReply`, and
`replyOwed` is `ReplyNeeded == 1 && ClassifyAsk(AsksFor) != AskFYI`. The
behaviour is unchanged for the profile's canonical spellings; the FYI veto now
matches the owner's case- and space-insensitive classification.

**Regressions.** `TestAsksOwnerReadsTheOneVocabulary` covers reply_needed,
answer_question (including mixed case and spaces), FYI (including mixed case),
concrete work, unknown, empty and automated. `TestReplyOwedReadsTheOneVocabulary`
covers the reply answer, the FYI veto in three spellings, and no answer.
`TestAskVocabularyLivesInThreadintel` refuses either literal outside
`ClassifyAsk` and pins one occurrence in the owner file.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the FYI veto back to the raw comparison
(`fyi veto is case-insensitive: replyOwed = true, want false`); the resolver
re-spelling the ask (`threadintel spells "answer_question" 2 times, want once`).

**Evidence.** `go vet`; `go test ./internal/threadintel ./internal/priority`
passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The two rules keep different structures: the resolver asks
"does this inbound message ask the owner", while priority asks "does this ranked
row owe a reply" and additionally vetoes FYI. Both now share the vocabulary, not
the whole predicate; merging them would change reported priority numbers, which
is a product decision, not a refactor. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One run-history read for five run tables

The store audit's ninth finding: `ListRuns`, `ListIndexRuns`, `ListEvidenceRuns`,
`ListLayer1Runs` and `ListTriageRuns` each spelled the same run-history read —
`id, started_at, finished_at, status, <columns>, error` ordered by `id DESC`
with `max(limit, 1)` — so a limit or ordering change had to reach five
functions, and the sync lister even ordered its columns differently.

`listRuns[T]` in `lists.go` now owns the frame, the order and the limit clamp;
each lister names only its table and its own columns. The sync SELECT was
reordered to the shared frame, and all five scans read the same positions.

**Regressions.** `TestRunListersShareOneQuery` requires each of the five
functions to call `listRuns` and to contain no `ORDER BY`, and pins one
definition. `TestRunListClampsItsLimit` seeds two index runs and requires
`ListIndexRuns(0)` and `ListIndexRuns(-5)` to return exactly one row.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the shared read dropping the clamp
(`ListIndexRuns(0) returned 0 rows`); one lister building its own query
(`evidence.go: … does not read through listRuns` / `builds its own run query`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store`; `go test ./internal/store` passes
(22.5 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `qa.go` keeps its own history reads because they carry a
conversation filter and two column sets; they are a different shape, not this
read. During the mutation check the evidence lister's restore backup was
missing, so the function was reconstructed against the shared reader and the
suite re-run; the five listers now all call it. The deployed build predates this
change.

## 2026-11-04 — One time window, two declared undated policies

The store audit's second finding: the `since`/`until` window was built in two
places and had drifted. Search guarded both bounds with `instant != ''`; the
mail-query builder did not, so an undated message fell inside an upper-bounded
mail window and outside the same search window.

`instantRange(where, args, since, until, undatedInside)` in `mailquery.go` now
owns the shape. Search passes `false` (an undated message is not "before" a
date), and the ranked mail query passes `true` because the company profile
documents that such a message still counts in Messages and Recent even though it
cannot enter a month bucket. The difference is a named contract at each call
site instead of two SQL spellings; `cachedCounterpartRows`, the Go side of the
same read, keeps the same inclusive rule and the existing parity test compares
both.

**Regressions.** `TestInstantRangeDeclaresUndatedMessages` pins the guard count
for search, the upper-only window, the unguarded mail window and the open
window. `TestInstantRangeCallersDeclareTheRule` pins each caller's flag. The
existing `TestCompanyProfilesMatchTheOrderedQuery` compares the Go filter with
the SQL for four windows, which is what caught the first, wrong unification:
a naive shared guard dropped undated messages from every profile window and the
parity oracle disagreed.

Mutations, each failing as intended: search switching to the inclusive rule
(`search.go does not declare … false`); the builder always guarding
(`profiles differ from the ordered query` and `a mail window excludes undated
messages, which the profile counts`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store`; `go test ./internal/store` passes
(19.3 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The inclusive/bounded split is a product contract, not a
derived fact: a future caller must choose a side and the guard test makes the
choice visible. The Go filter and the SQL must stay aligned; the profile parity
test is the cross-check. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One contact scan per company book

The store audit's fourth finding: every company-book rebuild read the whole
address book twice. `buildCompanyBookFrom` computed the contact fingerprint with
one stream of `companyContactRowsQuery`, saw it differ from the installed book,
and called `buildCompanyBook`, which streamed the same rows again and recomputed
the same per-row hashes.

`buildCompanyBook` now takes the digest the cache pass already computed. When
present it skips the per-row `companyContactRowHash` and stores the given value;
the first build (no previous book) still computes it from its own scan. The
address book is read once per rebuild, and the SHA per row runs once instead of
twice.

**Regression.** `TestCompanyBookKeepsTheComputedContactFingerprint` builds a
book, writes a contact, rebuilds, and requires the rebuilt book's stored
fingerprint to equal a fresh `companyBookContactFingerprint` of the same
generation. The existing `TestCompanyBookIsBuiltOncePerAddressBookGeneration`
still covers reuse across mail and label writes and the rebuild after a contact
or owner write.

Mutation, failing as intended: the build storing a zero digest instead of the
computed one (`rebuilt book stores contact fingerprint "000…0", want "c47c…"`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store`; `go test ./internal/store` passes
(21.0 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The two passes must agree about which rows they read: both
use `companyContactRowsQuery` with the snapshot's picked keys, and the fingerprint
pass has no ORDER BY because the XOR is order-independent. A caller that builds
a book with a fingerprint from a different snapshot would store a digest that
does not describe its rows; only `buildCompanyBookFrom` passes one, and it uses
the same snapshot for both. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One uint64 cursor parser

The API audit's sixth finding: the SSE `since` cursor repeated the
present/empty/`ParseUint` body that `queryUint` already had, with its own error
pair. The two had to stay in step or a client's cursor would be accepted by one
route and refused by the other.

`queryUint(r, name, invalid)` now takes the caller's problem constructor;
`nil` keeps the parameter's own `invalid_<name>` pair. `sseSince` calls it and
keeps only its `Last-Event-ID` fallback, and the logs route passes `nil`. The SSE
route keeps its longer "invalid since cursor" message, which is now a parameter
rather than a second parser.

**Regressions.** `TestQueryUintHasOneOwner` requires the SSE cursor to call
`queryUint` and to stop reading `r.URL.Query()["since"]`, and the logs route to
use the parser. `TestQueryUintShape` covers absent, zero, a value, empty,
malformed and negative input, and checks the SSE caller's own message survives.

Mutations, each failing as intended: an empty cursor accepted as zero
(`empty: err = <nil>, want invalid_since`); the SSE route parsing its own cursor
(`sseSince still reads the query itself`). A first attempt at the empty-value
mutation was behavior-preserving because `ParseUint("")` also fails, so it proved
nothing and was replaced.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` passes (3.5 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `queryUint` now treats an empty value as absent-shaped input
but still answers the invalid problem, matching both callers; the header fallback
in `sseSince` keeps its own `ParseUint` because it is not a query parameter. The
deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One settings-existence rule

The API audit's eighth finding: the settings detail, write and reset routes each
checked the key with their own `Get` + `ErrUnknownSetting()` pair, and two of

`requireSetting(key)` in `routes_settings.go` owns the rule and returns the

**Regressions.** `TestSettingExistenceHasOneOwner` requires one

Mutations, each failing as intended: the helper accepting an unknown key
(`TestEndpointMisuse/settings_unknown`: `status 200, want 404`); the detail route
re-checking the setting (`checks the setting 2 times, want once in
requireSetting`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` passes (3.3 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `requireSetting` returns a zero view alongside the error, so a
caller that ignores the error paints an empty setting instead of failing; the
three call sites return on error. A fourth route must call the same helper, which
the guard enforces by count. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One wire timestamp form

The API audit's ninth finding: `generated_at` was formatted in two handlers with
their own `time.RFC3339` call, while the other views receive a preformatted
string from their service. Two spellings of one wire fact, and a client that
parses the field in more than one shape.

`wireTime(t)` in `internal/api/wire.go` now owns the form: UTC, RFC 3339, no
fractional seconds. The priority page and the company profile batch both call
it; neither formats a timestamp itself.

**Regressions.** `TestWireTimeHasOneOwner` requires both routes to call
`wireTime` and refuses a local `Format(time.RFC3339)`, and pins the format rule
to one occurrence in `wire.go`. `TestWireTimeShape` checks a non-UTC instant
converted to `Z`, the zero instant, and that both outputs parse as RFC 3339.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the helper keeping the value's zone
(`wireTime(… +0100 CET) = "…+01:00", want "…Z"`); the priority route formatting
its own timestamp (`formats a timestamp itself; use wireTime`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` passes (3.3 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `wireTime` keeps the zero instant's own year
(`0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`) instead of inventing a value; a service that has no
timestamp yet should omit the field or set it explicitly. During this round
`wire.go` was overwritten by a shell redirect and restored from a worktree copy
of the same file (the thread view mappers and the two `nonNil` helpers); the
package builds, its full suite passes, and the list and thread wire tests cover
those helpers. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One label-queue query parser

The API audit's second finding: the label-queue query was parsed in two places —
the queue route and the message-binding branch of the message detail — and then
re-bounded a third time inside `labelQueueFor`. The two parsers had to stay in
step or a row could belong to a page the route would never serve.

`queryLabel(r)` in `routes_labels.go` now owns the shape: the bounded limit and
the strict review flag, with the question passed through. `handleLabelQueue`
parses once and `labelQueueFor` keeps only the queue's required-field rule; the
message binding parses the same way and treats any failure as the learning-gate
error. The redundant limit re-check in `labelQueueFor` is gone.

**Regressions.** `TestQueryLabelHasOneOwner` requires both files to call
`queryLabel`, pins the limit bound to one occurrence and refuses a returning
`query.Limit < 0` re-check. `TestQueryLabelShape` covers the default, a limit
and review, review off, the exact bound, past the bound, a negative limit and a
malformed review, each with its wire code.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the bound widened to `LabelQueueMax*100`
(`limit past bound: err = <nil>, want invalid_limit`); the limit re-bounded in
`labelQueueFor` (`labelQueueFor re-bounds the limit; queryLabel owns the bound`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` passes (5.5 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `queryLabel` no longer rejects a missing question itself; the
queue route still answers `invalid_request` for it and the binding maps it to the
gate error, so both surfaces keep their documented behaviour. `labelQueueFor`
would now pass an out-of-range limit to the service if another caller built a
`LabelQuery` by hand; no such caller exists, and the parser is the only
construction site. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One store filter and one role grammar

The API audit found the `store=` filter block copied verbatim in search and All
mail, and two role parsers that had already drifted: All mail accepted the
synthetic `all` population and treated `role=` as no filter, while search
rejected both. That difference was real, but nothing said so, so a change to one
page silently left the other behind.

`request.go` now owns both, beside `querySender`:

- `queryStore(r)` reads the optional mailbox-store filter and validates the key
  with `source.ValidStoreKey`.
- `queryRole(r, RoleGrammar{AllowAll, AllowEmpty})` reads the optional role.
  The grammar is a named value at each call site, so All mail says
  `{AllowAll: true, AllowEmpty: true}` and search passes `{}`. The drift is now a
  declared contract instead of an accident.

Both handlers read the owners and no longer touch `ValidStoreKey` or parse a
role themselves.

**Regressions.** `TestQueryStoreHasOneOwner` requires both route files to call
`queryStore` and to stop validating the key, and checks a bad key answers
`invalid_store` while an absent one is accepted. `TestQueryRoleGrammar` covers
all, empty, valid and invalid roles under both grammars plus the absent
parameter.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the store filter accepting any key
(`queryStore(bad key) = <nil>, want invalid_store`); the search grammar
accepting an empty role (`search empty: err = <nil>, want invalid_role`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` passes (3.3 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `RoleGrammar` has two booleans; a third page with a different
vocabulary should extend the named type rather than add a parameter. The
existing endpoint tests still pin both pages' wire codes, including search's
`role=all` and `role=` rejections. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One error mapper for every service sentinel

The API audit's top finding: four handlers carried their own error mapper —
`writeMessageListError`, the conversations inline switch, the thread inline
switch and `writeCommitmentsError` — each re-mapping service sentinels that
`mapError` already owns for other errors. A route that forgot the mapper
answered 500 for a validation failure.

All sixteen cases moved into `mapError`: the store page and thread sentinels
(invalid role, limit, store, sender, cursor, conversation id, thread cursor,
thread not found), the conversations filter sentinels (limit, cursor, state,
query) and the commitments sentinels (kind, direction, status, limit). The four
local mappers are deleted; every handler calls `writeError`. The redundant
`store.ErrNotFound` branch in the attachment route is gone as well, because
`mapError` already answers it.

**Regressions.** `TestServiceErrorsMapAtTheOneOwner` calls `mapError` for all
sixteen sentinels and requires the documented code and status, and refuses a
returning `writeMessageListError`/`writeCommitmentsError` function.
`TestGuardsHaveOneOwner` now pins the unknown-thread pair to `errors.go` and
refuses a hand-built 404 in the thread route.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `mapError` losing one moved sentinel
(`mapError(store: invalid message-list role) = 500 "internal", want 400
"invalid_role"`); a per-handler mapper returning (`a per-handler error mapper
writeMessageListError is back; extend mapError`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` passes (3.4 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `mapError` is now the single place that assigns these codes,
so a future route that wants a different code for the same sentinel must add a
parameter to the sentinel or handle it before `writeError`; silently shadowing
the mapping is what the guard refuses. The moved cases were behavior-preserving:
every existing endpoint test still asserts the same wire codes. The deployed
build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One owner per repeated API guard and 404 constructor

Four guards in `internal/api` were spelled twice, so a message change would have
reached only one route.

- `notFoundWith(code, message)` is now the one 404 constructor; `notFound()` and

- `requireHeldRemovals(w, r)` is the one availability guard of the two
  held-removal routes.

**Regressions.** `TestGuardsHaveOneOwner` pins each shared owner as exactly one

pins the five wire pairs (code, message, status 404) and `invalidBefore`.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a second held-removal guard
(`routes_held.go spells "held removals are unavailable" 2 times, want once`);
the cursor re-spelling the invalid pair (`lacks invalidParam(name)` and the
message literal twice).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` passes (6.1 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (80 s wall).

parameter whose code is not `invalid_<name>` must not use it; both current

The UI audit's third finding was a real label drift rather than a pure

`blockerSubjectText(blocker)` in `00-core.js` now owns the rule: the friendly

Mutations, each failing as intended: the helper returning the raw name always
(`blocker_subject failed: … Expected values to be strictly equal`); the rail

## 2026-11-04 — One metadata separator, owned by the i18n runtime

The UI audit's top finding: the metadata separator `" · "` had 29 owners across
24 modules, and one surface already put the string in the catalog
(`settings.resource_usage.separator`) while every other surface typed it.

`internal/ui/i18n.js` now owns the rule, next to `formatNumber` and
`localeCompare`: `metaSeparator()` reads the catalog key
`common.meta_separator` (renamed from the settings-specific key, identical in
both languages), and `metaLine(parts)` drops absent parts and joins the rest
with it. `00-core.js` destructures both, the local constant and helper are gone,
and every one of the 29 sites calls them: the problem diagnostic, the job strip
and its metrics, Home's mailbox and recent-question lines, the brief topic
coverage, Ask's citation and identity lines, Ask history, Learning progress,
Companies' loop and person meta, the Sources subtitle and picker, the Labels
judge button, the mail sender line and attachment badges, Important's capped
count, Search's suggestion and triage-reading lines, the action dialog's
detected zone, and the Settings resource readout.

**Regressions.** The existing suites cover the rendered strings (sender meta,
triage readings, resource limits, mailbox subtitle, diagnostics). The harnesses
that evaluate one marked section of `app.js` now wire `I.metaLine` and
`I.metaSeparator` beside `I.t`, the same way every other runtime function
reaches a sandbox, so the shared owner works in both the real bundle and the
per-module harnesses.

**Evidence.** `go generate ./internal/ui`; `go test ./internal/ui` passes;
`scripts/test-ui.sh` passes 179/179 (38.8 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all
fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `metaLine` drops empty parts, so two call sites that used to
build `name + " · " + absent` now render just the name instead of a trailing
separator; every such value is optional metadata and the tests assert the
present case. The separator is read from the catalog on each call, so a live
language switch keeps it current. The resource catalog test no longer lists the
separator key because the key is no longer resource copy; the catalog-parity
test still requires it in both languages. The deployed build predates this
change.

each carried a companies mock — `companyMocks` and `mockCompanies` — with the

`c:external` entry in one and an empty profile-summary route in the other.

`e2e/fixtures/companies.ts` owns `mockCompanies(page)`: the list view, the empty
profiles summary, and the three profile keys the specs select (acme, beta,
external), with an `unknown_company` 404 for anything else. Both specs import it
and their local copies are gone.

`TestE2EFixturesAreShared` gained the matching rule: no spec may define
`mockCompanies(` or `companyMocks(` again.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a spec defining its own companies mock
(`scoped-search.spec.ts defines its own companies mock`).

**Evidence.** `companies.spec.ts` and `scoped-search.spec.ts` pass (16 tests);
`scripts/test-ui.sh` passes 179/179 in 36.0 s; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all
fast checks passed (64 s wall).

**Residual risk.** The shared fixture now serves the empty profile-summary route
to the companies spec too, which only reads it on mount; the profiles it returns
are empty, as before. A test that needs a different list or a different profile
map still registers its own routes (four tests do). The extraction removed a
shared helper by accident on the first attempt and the affected specs caught it;
that helper is restored. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One data-directory owner in the scripts

The cmd/scripts audit's medium: the scripts resolved the app data directory in

`LOCALAPPDATA`), and `embed-local.sh` hard-coded the same directory plus

`gate_scripts` refuses a script that spells
`XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/mailsense` again.

provider resolution with `MAILSENSE_DATA_DIR` plus `PROVIDERS_FILE` (explicit
override, then the data-directory default) pass; the new gate invariant fails on
a planted copy. `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `runtime_data_dir` mirrors `config.ResolvePaths` and the app
remains the owner; a change to the app's path resolution still needs the mirror
updated, which the comment states. `provider_file` needs `jq` only when
`settings.json` exists, as before. Benchmark scripts that read
`EMBEDLOCAL_PROVIDERS` now see the configured provider file instead of a fixed
name, which is the documented contract. The deployed build predates this change.

(`visibleText("éè…")` differs from the 160-rune truncation).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/render`; `go test ./internal/render` passes;

renderer presentation cap, not a shared limit, and `truncateRunes` adds the

## 2026-11-04 — Shared e2e fixtures, and one flaky write counter

The cmd/scripts/e2e audit's medium: nine specs restated the boot status body
(`{ version: "e2e", time_zone: "UTC", data_dir: "/tmp/e2e" }`) and three specs
defined the same one-shot `deferred()` gate.

`fixtures/data.ts` now exports `statusView(overrides)`, and `fixtures/test.ts`
exports `deferred()`. The nine call sites and the three local definitions are
gone; a test overrides only the status field it asserts. A new guard,
`TestE2EFixturesAreShared`, scans `e2e/specs` and refuses either literal again.

The full browser suite then exposed a real flake in `labels.spec.ts`: after
`waitForRequest` resolves (the request was sent), the mocked route handler that
counts writes may not have run yet, so `expect(writes).toBe(1)` raced it under
eight workers. The two counters now use `expect.poll`, so the assertion waits
for the handler instead of the scheduler.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a spec restating the status body
(`timezone.spec.ts restates the status view`); a spec defining its own deferred
(`performance.spec.ts defines its own deferred gate`).

**Evidence.** The seven affected specs pass (41 tests, 13.7 s); the full
`scripts/test-ui.sh` passes (179/179, 21.0 s) after the flake fix;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `statusView` returns a plain record, so a test that mutates
the result keeps its own copy; the overrides are shallow. The labels poll waits
up to the default expect timeout for the handler, so a genuinely missing write
still fails, just later than before. The remaining e2e duplication (the settings
catalog, the companies mocks, the shared server helpers) is untouched and is the
next target. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — The maintenance intervals read their schema defaults

The cmd/scripts audit's medium: two catch-up intervals restated the schema
default in code. `triageCatchUpDefault = 5 * time.Minute` in cmd and an inline
`interval = 5 * time.Minute` in the store worker both duplicated
`triage.auto.interval` (default 5m, min 30s) and
`store.maintenance_interval` (default 5m, min 1m). The schema owns both values,
so a schema change would have left the worker on the old cadence.

`triage.AutoInterval(cfg)` now resolves the catch-up interval next to
`AutoBatch`; the cmd triage worker calls it and the constant is gone. The store
worker passes `cfg.Duration(store.SettingMaintainEvery)` directly and its
fallback is removed.

**Regressions.** `TestAutoIntervalFollowsTheSetting` requires the schema's
positive default and then a live `90s` override, so a literal in the accessor
fails. `TestMaintenanceIntervalsHaveNoLocalDefault` requires the two cmd workers
to read their accessors and to keep no `5 * time.Minute` or
`triageCatchUpDefault`.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `AutoInterval` returning a literal 5m
(`AutoInterval = 5m0s, want the live 90s`); the store worker re-adding the
fallback (`storemaintenance.go keeps "5 * time.Minute"`).

**Evidence.** `go vet`; `go test ./internal/triage` (10.9 s) and
`go test ./cmd/mailsense` pass; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks
passed.

**Residual risk.** As with `AutoBatch`, the workers now trust the schema's
minimum: a config value of 0 would make `maintainTriage`/`storeMaintain` loop on
a zero interval (the ticker would spin). `config.Load` applies the schema
defaults and minimum, and the tests pin the default, so the path is unreachable
through the supported loader. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — The attachment read uses the one transport owner

The UI audit's third medium: `inlineAssetURL` in `30-mail-body.js` called `fetch`
directly with its own `Authorization` header, its own 401 branch and no timeout
or abort, so an attachment read could hang past `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, and a 401
during image hydration followed a second, weaker path than every API read.

`request` now takes `as: "blob"` (and an explicit `cache`), keeping its one
abort/timeout, token header, 401 handling and error mapping; a blob response
skips the text and JSON parse and returns the body. `inlineAssetURL` is one
`request(..., { as: "blob", cache: "default" })` call plus the image MIME
allow-list and `URL.createObjectURL`; the local fetch, 401 branch and
`asset <status>` error are gone.

**Regressions.** `TestRequestOwnsTimeout` now requires
`cache: options.cache || "no-store"` (the default policy is unchanged) and adds
two guards: `30-mail-body.js` must call `request` with
`{ as: "blob", cache: "default" }` and must not contain `fetch(`, so the
attachment path cannot leave the transport owner again. The existing e2e spec
"HTML body keeps sender layout, compiles its CSS and hydrates inline images"
covers the happy path through a real browser.

**Evidence.** `go generate ./internal/ui`; `go test ./internal/ui` passes;
`scripts/test-ui.sh` passes (179/179, 25.1 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all
fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** The blob branch maps a non-2xx response to
`ApiError(http_<status>)` instead of the old plain `Error("asset …")`; the only
caller marks the placeholder missing either way, and a 401 still ends on the
token screen through `handleUnauthorized`. The cache override is the only one in
the client, pinned by the guard. The deployed build predates this change.

Four lows from the installprofile/messages and vector/jsonx audits, each a fact
with a second owner.

**Desktop title.** `bootstrapPage` typed `Mailsense` twice (the page title and the
link) while `desktop.WindowTitle` owns it. The page now reads the constant for

`TestSealUsesTheStdlibKeyIterator` refuses a new hand-rolled iterator.
`TestPrecisionComesFromTheCounts` covers a first and a second `finish`, the

(`seal.go re-implements map keys`). The first desktop mutation only changed

redone mutation spells the page literal and changes the constant.

older store (its documented reason). The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One finiteness predicate and one raw short hash

Two of the vector/jsonx/mathx/digest audit's lows, both a shared rule spelled in
more than one package.

**Finiteness.** `optim.finite`, `jsonx.Finite` and `vector.Check` each tested
`!math.IsNaN(x) && !math.IsInf(x, 0)`. `mathx.IsFinite(v)` now owns it; the
optimizer (lbfgs and line search), the JSON number rule and the vector
trust-boundary check all call it, and the local predicate is deleted.

**Raw short hash.** `digest.Hex` kept its own `sha256.Sum256` +
`hex.EncodeToString`, and `fixturetest.Key` built the 8-byte map key with a
second hand-rolled `sha256.Sum256`. `digest.Sum(data, n)` is now the raw prefix,
`Hex` is the hex form of `Sum`, and `Key` is `[8]byte(digest.Sum(input, 8))`.

**Regressions.** `TestIsFinite` covers zero, subnormals, ±MaxFloat64, NaN and both
infinities; `TestFinitenessIsSpelledOnce` scans `jsonx`, `optim` and `vector` and
refuses a file that still contains both `IsNaN` and `IsInf`.
`TestSumIsTheRawHexPrefix` requires `Sum` to be a prefix of the full digest for
every length, including 0, 32 and beyond, and `Hex` to equal its hex form.
`TestKeyIsTheDigestSumPrefix` requires the cache key to equal `digest.Sum(input,
8)` and `vectorcache.go` to stop importing `crypto/sha256`.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `IsFinite` returning true
(`IsFinite(NaN) = true`); jsonx re-spelling the pair (`../jsonx/number.go keeps
its own finiteness pair`); `Sum` ignoring the length (`Sum(data, 1) has 32
bytes, want 1`); the key dropping a byte (`Key(...)` mismatch).

matching `Hex`'s documented clamp; a caller that wants exactly `n` bytes must
pass a valid `n`. `mathx.IsFinite` takes a `float64`, so the vector check widens
`float32` first, which is exact. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — Test time: the layer1 suite runs in parallel

Layer1 was the longest package in the gate (37.6 s under load, 29 s standalone):
183 top-level tests, none calling `t.Parallel()`, so they ran one after another.
The package-level values are read-only tables (`experiments`, `purposes`,
`testFit`, `testKey`), the route-key memo is mutex-guarded, and no test uses
`t.Setenv`, `os.Chdir` or a flag, so the tests are independent.

Every top-level layer1 test now calls `t.Parallel()` first. The suite passes
`-race -count=2` (104 s) with no data race, and `go test ./internal/layer1`
drops from 29 s to 6.8 s (4.3x).

**Evidence.** `-race -count=2` green; `go test ./internal/layer1` 6.8 s;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` green with the parallel suite in shard B.

**Residual risk.** Parallel tests share the process CPU and the Go build cache;
a future test that mutates one of the package-level tables or a global seam would
now be a race, so such a test must be kept serial (or the seam replaced). The
`-race` run is the guard. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — Test time: one migrated database for the store suite

The store suite's helper `open` ran 37 migrations, the full-text index setup and
the startup passes on a brand-new file for every one of the suite's ~295 opens:
25.6 s standalone, 36 s inside the gate.

`migratedTemplate` (a `sync.OnceValues` in `testdb_test.go`) builds one migrated,
empty database in a process-lifetime temp directory, closes it (which
checkpoints the WAL) and keeps its bytes. `open` copies those bytes into the
test's own data directory before `Open`, so every test still owns a private
database while the migrations run once per test binary.

**Evidence.** `go test ./internal/store` passes in 15.8 s (was 25.6 s, 1.6x);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` passes in 79 s with all shards and the race pair green.

**Regressions.** The template is built by `Open` itself, so a newly added
migration is applied to it automatically; the existing
`TestOpenMigratesAndIsIdempotent`-style assertions on `user_version` and the
fresh-path tests keep covering the migration chain. A test that needs a corrupt
or future-version database does not go through `open`, so it still starts from
its own file.

**Residual risk.** The template is built with default settings; a per-test
override that changes DB-visible startup (`store.synchronous`, preview mode)
still applies at that test's `Open`, and the copied file carries only the schema
and the `meta` rows `recordOpen` writes (`created_at`/`created_version`, kept on
conflict). The template build costs one extra open per test process. The
deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — Test time: measured cuts across the three gates

The user asked to cut testing time by 25x. Measured baseline on this host: the
exhaustive `scripts/test.sh` took about 14 minutes (`-p 1` and `-race` over every
package, recorded in this log), the browser suite 90 s (`179 passed (1.5m)`), and
the fast gate 94 s. Changes, each measured:

**Browser suite 90 s → 21.7 s (4.1x, 179/179 passed).**
- `playwright.config.ts`: 2 workers → 8 on a 12-core host (4 on CI).
- `boot.spec.ts`: one navigation per route, then a resize per viewport, instead
  of reloading every route for every width (70 navigations → 10); the fixed
  60 ms settle is two `requestAnimationFrame`s.
- `mail.spec.ts`: the three TTL branches advance `page.clock` instead of sleeping
  out 15.5 s, 8 s + 9 s and 20.5 s; the 26.8 s stale-cache test is now 6.8 s.
- `fixtures/sse.ts`: `installFakeStreamWithClock` is the one fake-stream-plus-
  clock setup for those tests (mail.spec stays at its 1759-line ratchet budget).
- A spec-wide clock in `completion-events.spec.ts` was tried and reverted: one
  test then saw an extra `/api/messages` read, so the real 1.5 s settle stays.

**Fast gate 94 s → 71 s.**
- `test-lib.sh`: the ten vet configurations run concurrently instead of
  sequentially, each output replayed only on failure.
- Every `go test` call adds `-vet=off`: `gate_vet` already owns vet, and the test
  binary's own vet pass was a duplicate.
- `test-fast.sh`: the `-race` qa+api check is a fourth shard started beside A, B
  and C instead of after them.

**Exhaustive gate ~14 min → 75 s.**
- `test.sh` runs one `go test` over every package with `-p 8` instead of `-p 1`,
  and `-vet=off`.
- Race coverage is its own gate: `scripts/test-race.sh` is `test.sh` with
  `RACE=on`, and `test.sh` now defaults `RACE=off`. The fast gate still runs
  `-race` on qa and api on every round; the full race matrix is the release
  check rather than the inner loop.

**Evidence.** `scripts/test-fast.sh` passes (71 s); `scripts/test.sh` passes
(75 s); `scripts/test-ui.sh` passes (179/179, 21.7 s).

**Residual risk.** `RACE=off` in `test.sh` moves exhaustive race coverage to
`scripts/test-race.sh`; a release must run both. Ten concurrent vet builds spike
CPU and memory, which is why the verifier's own resource-guard tests are not run
in that phase. The clock-driven mail tests freeze page time after the fixture
sets it; the completion-events spec was not converted because the change altered
an event-coalescing assertion. The remaining wall floor is the isolated sidecar
suite (28 s) and the store package; both are the next measured targets.

## 2026-11-04 — One pacing loop for the resource guard

The jobs/events/safe audit's first finding: `resource.Guard.Wait` and
`jobs.Manager.pace` both implemented the same "re-check the ceiling every
interval until it clears" loop. `Wait` had no production caller; the live loop
was `pace`, so the guard's own hysteresis, interval and admission class were
stepped twice and could drift.

`Guard.WaitAdmission(ctx, admission, onChange)` now owns the loop: it polls
`CheckAdmission`, hands the current ceiling to `onChange` on entry and nil once
the host recovers, sleeps on the guard's own clock and interval, and returns the
last stopping ceiling. `Wait` is `WaitAdmission(ctx, AdmitAll, nil)`.
`Manager.pace` is one call with `setPaused` as the reporter, so a job publishes
exactly its pause and resume and nothing re-spells the cadence.

**Regressions.** `TestWaitAdmissionReportsEveryTransition` requires the callback
to see paused, paused, resumed across two fake-clock intervals.
`TestWaitAdmissionRespectsTheAdmissionClass` requires an `AdmitWrites` job to
ignore a CPU ceiling and still hear the resumed state.
`TestWaitSleepsUntilTheHostRecovers` (the old `Wait` contract) and the jobs
`TestReportPausesUntilHostRecovers` (pause/resume events and sleep count) still
pin the shared path.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the loop no longer reporting the resume
(`transitions = [paused, paused], want paused, paused, resumed`); the loop
sleeping on a real timer instead of the guard's clock (the fake clock records no
sleeps and the test times out, which is also why the suite now bounds every test
binary).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/resource ./internal/jobs`; both suites pass;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` passes in 94 s wall.

**Residual risk.** `pace` now uses the guard's clock instead of the manager's.
Production wires both to the wall clock and every jobs test passes one fake to
both, so no behaviour changes; a future caller that gives them different clocks
would pace on the guard's. `WaitAdmission` reports the ceiling on every poll, not
only on a transition; `setPaused` already collapses equal pauses, which keeps the
event stream unchanged. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — The log service follows configuration through the one subscriber

The jobs/events/safe audit's fourth finding: `events.On` documents itself as "the
one subscribe-and-loop of the codebase", yet `logx.Service` kept a
`Subscription`, a `WaitGroup` and its own `follow` loop, with a `Close` that had
to unsubscribe and wait by hand.

`Setup` now installs the follower with
`events.On(bus, config.TopicChanged, snap.EventBuffer(), s.followChange)`,
stores the returned stop, and `Close` calls it (unsubscribe, then wait for the
in-flight handler). The `sub` and `wg` fields and the `follow` method are gone;
`followChange(change)` keeps the per-key filter and the single apply.

**Regressions.** `TestCloseStopsFollowingConfiguration` subscribes to
`TopicApplied`, applies one live change, closes the service, publishes another,
and requires no further apply within 100 ms: an unclosed follower would still
observe the bus. `TestLogxFollowsThroughEventsOn` requires exactly one `events.On`
call in `service.go` and no `events.Subscribe` (generic instantiation included),
`sync.WaitGroup`, `s.sub` or `s.wg`.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `Close` not calling the stop
(`a configuration change was applied after Close`); a generic
`events.Subscribe[config.Change]` surviving next to `events.On`
(`service.go still keeps "events.Subscribe"`). The first guard version used
`events.Subscribe(` and missed the generic form; the substring is now the package
path without the parenthesis.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/logx`; `go test ./internal/logx` passes
(1.7 s) including `TestLiveReconfiguration`; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all
fast checks passed.

**Residual risk.** `events.On` starts its goroutine at subscribe time, so a
change published between subscribe and `Setup`'s first `apply` can apply twice
(serialised by `apply`'s mutex); the previous order subscribed before applying
too, so the window is unchanged. A bus that is closed mid-setup still returns
`ErrClosed` from `On`, handled like the old subscribe. The deployed build predates
this change.

## 2026-11-04 — The job manager joins through the one join owner

The jobs/events/safe audit's second medium: `jobs.Manager` carried its own
`closed` flag, its own `sync.WaitGroup` and a hand-rolled bounded join in
`Shutdown`, while `join.Group` is the documented owner used by api, world,
viewcache, sidecar, learning, search and messages.

`Manager` now holds a `join.Group`: `Start` admits a job through `Track` (false →
`ErrShutdown`, the same answer the closed flag gave), `run` retires it with
`Done`, `CancelAll` calls `Refuse` (refuse admission, then cancel the live jobs),
and `Shutdown` is `CancelAll` plus `Close(ctx)`. The `closed` field and the
`WaitGroup` are gone.

`join.Close` also took over the manager's one real semantic difference: after
waking on the caller's context it takes a second look at the drain, so a join
that finished in the same instant is reported joined. That look is
`joined(done)`, a small function the test can drive directly (the window itself
is timing-dependent and cannot be forced through the public API).

**Regressions.** `TestShutdownJoinsThroughTheGroup` requires a started job to be
tracked, `Shutdown` to join it and leave the group at zero, the next `Start` to be
refused with `ErrShutdown`, and a refused `Start` to track nothing.
`TestJoinedSeesADrainTheSelectMissed` requires the second look to read a closed
drain as joined and an open one as unjoined, and requires `Close`'s context
branch to call it. `TestCloseReportsAnUnjoinedTaskWhenContextEnds` keeps the real
unjoined answer for an active task. The existing
`TestShutdownCancelsAndRefuses`, `TestShutdownJoinsACooperativeExpiredBody` and
`TestShutdownStillJoinsAfterADeadline` stay as the contract of the manager.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `Start` no longer tracking the job
(`TestShutdownCancelsAndRefuses`: `job-1: running`); `joined` always returning
false (`a closed drain was reported unjoined`); `Close`'s context branch
returning false (`Close's context branch does not re-check the drain`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/join ./internal/jobs`; both suites pass;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed, including the `-race`
qa+api pair that exercises the API's join.

**Residual risk.** `Start` calls `Track` while holding the manager mutex; the
group takes its own lock and never calls back into the manager, so the ordering
is one-way. `Shutdown` no longer waits on a `WaitGroup`, so a job body that
outlives its deadline finalizer is bounded by the group exactly as before (the
deadline finalizer still ends the record). The broadened `Close` answer applies
to every owner of a `Group`: a drain finishing at the context boundary now
reports joined rather than unjoined. The deployed build predates this change.

")` and the same `details.blocker-diagnostic` block with `common.diagnostic` and
