it and no longer spell `problem.stage, problem.subject, problem.message`, and
`TestGeneratedBundlesAreCurrent` requires the committed bundles to match the
sources.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the error screen re-inlining the block
(`52-init.js builds its own problem line; call problemDiagnostic`); the helper
dropping the subject (`problemDiagnostic does not join the three problem
fields`).

**Evidence.** `go generate ./internal/ui`; `go test ./internal/ui` (bundle and
renderer tests) passes; `scripts/test-ui.sh` passes (179 Playwright specs); the
exporter and toast paths are covered by the error-screen and completion specs;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

`diagnostic` string, the Ask answer, the Sources backfill, the Labels blocker and

shows "Hub" for "screen.hub.title"; the English catalog says "Home"`); an element
losing its fallback text (`index.html shows "" for "shell.updating"; the English

**Evidence.** `scripts/test-ui.sh` passes (179 Playwright specs, 1.5 m, shell,

tests pass; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed.

## 2026-11-04 — One declared list behind the scope enums

The installprofile/messages/mailquery audit's fourth medium: `scope.Reason` had a
const block of ten reasons and a hand-written `switch` that listed the same ten
again, and `Verdict` compared its three values inline. `store/scope.go` rejects
any reason `Valid` refuses, so a rule added to `Decide` without a second edit to
the switch would have failed every scope write at runtime, silently.

`allReasons` and `allVerdicts` are now the one list each, and `Valid` is
`slices.Contains` over it. The const block stays the vocabulary; `verdict.go`'s
AST guard keeps the two in step.

**Regressions.** `TestEveryReasonIsValidAndUnique` requires every listed reason
and verdict to be valid, no duplicates, and an undeclared value to be invalid.
`TestReasonConstantsMatchTheList` parses `verdict.go`, counts the `Reason` and
`Verdict` constants in its const blocks, and requires the counts to equal the
lists: adding a rule without listing it fails the test instead of the write.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a constant missing from `allReasons` (`10
Reason constants, 9 entries in allReasons: list the new rule`); a repeated entry
(`reason "sent_by_owner" is listed twice` plus the count mismatch).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/scope`; `go test ./internal/scope` passes;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The AST guard counts constants; a reason built as a
non-constant expression (for example `Reason("x_" + suffix)`) would not be
counted, and none exists today. `Decide` can still return a reason that is
listed but wrong for the evidence; the list answers "is this a known rule", not
"is this rule correct for this message", which the decision tests cover. The
deployed build predates this change.

The cmd/scripts/e2e audit's first high: `cmd/mailsense/main.go` read

`agenda.SettingDefaultHours` now owns the key and main.go builds

Mutations, each failing as intended: the constant misspelled as
`agenda.default_hour` (the test panics with `config: unknown setting
"agenda.default_hour"`); main.go spelling the literal again (`main.go reads the
setting cfg.Int("agenda.default_hours") inline; use the owning package's
constant`).

**Evidence.** `go vet`; `go test ./internal/agenda` and `go test ./cmd/mailsense`
pass; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87

## 2026-11-04 — One automatic triage batch, owned by the schema

The cmd/scripts/e2e audit's second high: the automatic triage batch size had
three answers. The schema declares `triage.auto.batch` with default `500` and
minimum `1`; `internal/triage`'s trigger and `cmd/mailsense`'s catch-up loop each
clamped a value below 1 to `100`. With a live config the clamp is unreachable
(the schema applies its default), but the second number disagreed with the owner
and would have shortened every automatic run had the schema default ever been
nulled.

`triage.AutoBatch(cfg)` is now the one resolution and returns
`cfg.Int(SettingBatch)` with no second default. `syncTrigger.options()` and the
cmd catch-up both call it, and the catch-up's clamp is gone.

**Regressions.** `TestAutoBatchReadsTheSchemaDefault` loads
`config.Defaults()`, requires the schema value to be at least 1, requires
`AutoBatch` to return exactly it (so no literal can drift), and requires the
trigger's resolved `Options.Limit` to be the same value.
`TestTriageMaintenanceHasNoSecondBatchDefault` requires
`triagemaintenance.go` to call `triage.AutoBatch(a.cfg)` and to keep neither
`batch = 100` nor a `SettingBatch` read.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the resolver returning a literal `100`
(`AutoBatch = 100, want the schema default 500`); the catch-up re-adding the
clamp (`triagemaintenance.go keeps "batch = 100"`).

**Evidence.** `go vet`; `go test ./internal/triage` (19.1 s) and
`go test ./cmd/mailsense` pass; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks
passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `AutoBatch` now trusts the schema minimum: a config value of 0
would mean an unbounded automatic run (`Options.Limit > 0` is what caps the
plan). The schema's `min: 1` makes that unreachable through `config.Load`, and
the regression test pins the default, not the minimum. The catch-up still reads
the batch once at startup, while the sync trigger reads it per run; that
difference predates this round. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One control-character decision at every boundary

The installprofile/messages/mailquery audit's third medium: the control-character
predicate existed three times. `calendar.isControl` and `mailquery.hasControl`
both spelled `r < 0x20 || r == 0x7f`, while `contacts.Valid` used
`unicode.IsControl`. The two copies therefore accepted U+0080..U+009F in calendar
attendees and Ask filters, and the contact path refused them: one rule, three
answers.

`mail.HasControl(s)` now owns it as `strings.ContainsFunc(s, unicode.IsControl)`,
covering C0, DEL and the C1 range. `mailquery` uses it for `Contact`, `Text` and
every `ContactAddresses` entry; `calendar.Event.Validate` uses it for attendee
addresses and names; `contacts.Valid` uses it for addresses. The two local
predicates are deleted.

**Regressions.** `TestHasControlCoversC0DelAndC1` sweeps U+0000..U+009F and
requires the predicate to equal `unicode.IsControl` exactly.
`TestNoAsciiOnlyControlPredicate` scans the three consumer packages' production
files and refuses `r < 0x20`. `TestEventRejectsC1Control`,
`TestPlanRejectsC1Control` and `TestValidRejectsC1Control` require the C1 range to
be refused at each boundary and normal values to pass.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the owner falling back to the ASCII-only
predicate (`HasControl(U+0080) = false, want true`, plus
`a U+0080 control in an attendee name was accepted`); calendar re-spelling its
own predicate (`../calendar/calendar.go keeps an ASCII-only control predicate;
use mail.HasControl`).

**Evidence.** `go vet` and the full suites of `mail`, `calendar`, `mailquery` and
`contacts` pass; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet
configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `contacts.CleanPhone` still strips control characters with
`unicode.Map`; that is a cleaning operation (drop, then bound the length), not a
validation decision, and it already used the same `unicode.IsControl` rule.
Tightening calendar and Ask to C1 is a behaviour change: a message whose filter
carries U+0080..U+009F is now refused where it used to pass. The deployed build
predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One validation rule for the two ranked query kinds

The installprofile/mailquery/route audit's second medium: `Plan.Validate` wrote
the contacts and companies branches as the same five checks (rank action, a
known direction, a contact metric, no time grouping, the kind's limit), with
only the noun and the bound differing. The direction predicate was then spelled
a third and fourth time for messages and time, and the "non-empty window" rule
existed twice with two different messages.

Now:
- `planError` is the one trust-boundary error constructor (`Validate` binds it
  as `bad`).
- `validateRankedEntity(singular, plural, maxLimit)` owns the shared five checks;
  contacts and companies call it with their noun forms and their bound.
- `validDirection()` owns the three direction values, read by contacts,
  companies, messages and time.
- `windowError(since, until, sinceFull, untilFull)` owns "not backwards, and two
  full timestamps must not name the same instant"; `Validate` and `Resolve` both
  call it, so `Resolve`'s separate "since must be before until" message is gone.
- `MaxContactAddressChars` is `mail.MaxSenderQueryRunes`, and the check counts
  runes instead of bytes, matching the mail owner's address bound.

through both kinds and requires the kind's own noun in each error, plus the bound
limit passing; `TestDirectionRuleIsOneRule` requires all four kinds to accept the
three directions and refuse an unknown one; `TestWindowRuleIsOneRule` requires
`Validate` and `Resolve` to refuse a reversed pair and a same-instant full pair
with identical messages, and an inclusive same-day date pair to stay valid;
`TestContactAddressBoundCountsRunes` requires a 320-rune address that is over 640
bytes to pass and 321 runes to fail.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the ranked rule dropping the group check
(`Validate = <nil>, want "contacts cannot group by time"`); the direction rule
forgetting sent/received (`with direction "sent": invalid direction`); the window
rule dropping the empty-instant check (`Validate = <nil>, want "… non-empty
window"`); the address bound counting bytes (`a 320-rune address was refused`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/mailquery`; `go test ./internal/mailquery`
passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `Resolve` passes `true, true` for the fullness flags because
its bounds are already expanded; a caller that reaches `Resolve` without
`Validate` now gets the `Validate` wording. The ranked noun forms are explicit
arguments (English plurals are not derived), so a third ranked kind must pass its
own pair. The deployed build predates this change.

`TestWriteMakesAPrivateDirectoryAndFiles` covers the missing-directory path and
the `0600` file mode. `TestOpenVectorCacheRepairsTheDirectoryPerm` requires the
same `0755`-to-`0700` repair for the fixture cache.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the exporter creating the directory with
`os.MkdirAll(dir, 0o755)` (`export dir mode = 755, want 700`); the cache doing
the same (`cache dir mode = 755, want 700`). The exporter mutation first passed,

with `DirPerm`; a pre-existing parent above the leaf is not repaired, which is
the documented contract and unchanged here. The deployed build predates this
change.

## 2026-11-04 — One refusal vocabulary for the CSS compiler

The vector/jsonx/mathx/render audit's security-relevant medium: the CSS
presentation compiler kept the dangerous-fragment list three times —
`safeSelector` and `safeMediaQuery` each held the identical nine tokens inline,
and `safeValue` held a partly different list. A token added to one copy would
have passed the other two.

`dangerousCSS` (at-rule, `url(`, `expression`, `javascript:`, backslash, braces,
tag delimiters) and `dangerousValueCSS` (computed values and bindings:
`behavior:`, `-moz-binding`, `var(`, `attr(`, `env(`, `calc(`) are now the two
declarations in `style.go`, and `containsAny` is the one matcher.
`safeSelector`, `safeMediaQuery` and `safeValue` read them instead of holding
copies. `@` now covers `@import` in a value, so the redundant `@import` token is
gone; every value that previously reached the per-property validator with a
stray `@` was refused there anyway, so the tightening changes no accepted
output.

**Regressions.** `TestDangerousCSSIsOneSet` pins the two vocabularies as an
independent contract (a removed token fails loudly instead of shrinking the
test), requires all three validators to refuse every shared token and the value
validator to refuse every value-only token, and keeps a valid selector, media
query and value passing. `TestDangerousCSSIsSpelledOnce` requires both
declarations and the three `containsAny` call sites to exist exactly once, and
the shared list to be one literal.

Mutations, each failing as intended: dropping `javascript:` from the shared list
(`dangerousCSS = […]`, `want […]`); the value validator no longer reading
`dangerousValueCSS` (`style.go mentions … 0 time(s)`); the selector keeping a
private list (`safeSelector accepted a selector containing "expression"`). The
first mutation initially passed, which exposed the test iterating the production
slice it was checking; the independent contract list is the fix.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/render`; `go test ./internal/render` passes;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `dangerousValueCSS` remains defence in depth: the per-property
validators (`safeColor`, `safeFont`, `safeLengths`, `safeGeneric`) already refuse
every token's characters, so the behavioural test cannot distinguish a missing
value-only token from a later refusal; the contract and call-site guards do. The
token set is a fixed vocabulary, not a CSS grammar: a new function or at-rule
family needs a deliberate token. The deployed build predates this change.

The installprofile/messages/mailquery/route audit's top finding: the
trust-boundary validation of an offer list was written twice, verbatim. `Decide`

they wrapped the error (`ErrInvalid`/`Decide` vs `item %d`/`checkItem`).

`checkOffers(offers []Offer, classes int) error` now owns the rule: a known
layer, one offer per layer, and a distribution summing to 1 within

`route_test.go` stay as they are (they cover the two entry points' different
wrapping); the new table drives the one rule directly.

three. A rule added to one caller can no longer pass the others.

(`checkOffers = <nil>, want "offered twice"`); `checkItem` returning `nil` (six

Two of the config/index/syncer/learning audit's index lows, kept in one round
because both are report/stage facts of the same package.

**One attempted count.** `Report.Attempted()` now owns
`Embedded + Unchanged + Failed`. `progress()` publishes it as `Done`, and
`finish` derives `NotAttempted = Selected - Attempted()`, so the parts add up to
the selected count by construction instead of by three matching expressions.

blocked-by-embedder answer (code `no_embedder`, the `choose_embedder` action),

sites had built the same code and the same remedy by hand.

reports and then runs a real four-message index run and requires
`Attempted() + NotAttempted == Selected`.
`TestNoEmbedderBlockerIsOneAnswer` pins the code, detail and the single action,
and requires `stage.go` to build that blocker exactly once.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `Attempted()` dropping failures
(`Attempted() = 4, want 5`); `NotAttempted` losing one
(`attempted 4 + not attempted -1 != selected 4` in a real run); the helper
offering another remedy (`blocker actions [{ID:pick_mailboxes}]`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/index`; `go test ./internal/index` passes
(9.0 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87

**Residual risk.** `NotAttempted` stays a persisted field (the wire contract),
computed in `finish`; a producer that builds a `Report` by hand can still set it

deployed build predates this change.

`sync.Once` and the wait); `stopChild` only fixes which grace and clock reach
it. A future path that must stop a child with another grace can call `stop`
directly, but the source guard makes that a deliberate, visible edit. The
deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One value contract for the two secret stores

The secrets/fsx/sidecar/locale audit's secrets low: the file store and the
environment store each spelled "read a value from the map, a missing name is
`ErrNotFound`" and "list the names, sorted", and the file store spelled the
absence check a third time in `Delete`.

`internal/secrets/values.go` now owns both:

```go
func lookup(values map[string]string, name string) (string, error) // missing -> ErrNotFound
func sortedNames(values map[string]string) []string                // the one list order
```

`fileStore.Get`/`Delete`/`List` and `envStore.Get`/`List` call them; each store
keeps its own locking (the file store locks, the environment store does not), so
there is no variant flag and no shared lock. `slices`/`maps` imports dropped
where they became unused.

**Regressions.** `TestStoresShareOneValueContract` runs the same table against
both stores: a missing name is `ErrNotFound` (and an invalid name is a
validation error, not absence), a present name returns its value, and `List`
returns the exact sorted order for values written in a different order.
`TestValuePlumbingHasOneWriter` requires no store to read `s.values[name]`
inline and `values.go` to keep the one map read.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `lookup` returning `("", nil)` for a
missing name (`a missing name answered <nil>, want ErrNotFound`, both stores);
`sortedNames` reversing (`List = [CHARLIE_KEY BRAVO_KEY ALPHA_KEY]`); the
environment store re-spelling its read (`the stores read their map inline in
[envstore.go]`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/secrets`; `go test ./internal/secrets` passes;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The two stores still differ by design in mutability
(`fileStore` writes and is not read-only, `envStore` is read-only) and in
locking; `lookup`/`sortedNames` cover only the map plumbing. The deployed build
predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One parent-directory step for the root-confined writers

The secrets/fsx/sidecar/locale audit's fsx low: `WriteStreamIn` and `SymlinkIn`
each created a nested name's parent with the same root-relative `MkdirAll` block.
That block is the confinement boundary (the root-relative call is what keeps the
directory inside the archive root), so it is not a place for a second copy.

`fsx.mkdirParentIn(root, name)` now owns it: a name at the root needs no
directory, a nested name gets its parents with `DirPerm` through `root`. Both
`WriteStreamIn` and `SymlinkIn` call it; the duplicate blocks are gone.

**Regressions.** `TestRootWritersCreateTheirParent` writes a top-level file and
a nested one through `WriteStreamIn`, links a nested name through `SymlinkIn`,
and checks the bytes, the created parent, its `DirPerm`, and the link target;
`TestRootParentCreationHasOneWriter` scans the non-test sources and requires
exactly one `root.MkdirAll(` call in the package, inside `stream.go`.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `SymlinkIn` skipping its parent
(`SymlinkIn("links/deep/l"): symlinkat target links/deep/l: no such file or
directory`); `WriteStreamIn` re-spelling the block
(`root.MkdirAll is written in map[stream.go:2]; one call belongs to
mkdirParentIn`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/fsx`; `go test ./internal/fsx` passes;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `mkdirParentIn` creates parents only; the directory's own
mode is the one `root.MkdirAll` applies (`DirPerm`), and it does not repair an
existing directory's mode the way `EnsureDir` does for the data directory. The
deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One rule for the single white-space separator

The secrets/fsx/sidecar/locale audit's locale low: "skip one white-space token
of exactly one character" was written twice, as a helper in `currency.go` and
again inline in `pattern.match`. The rule is a property of the token stream, not
of either matcher.

`locale.space(tks, i)` now lives in `tokens.go` beside `joins`, `runWhile` and
`standaloneAt`. `currency.go`'s `amount` and `currency` calls are unchanged;
`pattern.go`'s `e.space` branch is now `i = space(tks, i)`; the copy in
`currency.go` is gone.

**Regressions.** `TestSpaceSkipsOneWhiteSpaceCharacter` covers one space, a
two-space run (one token of two characters, not skipped), a tab, no space and an
index past the end. `TestPatternSeparatorIsOneSpace` compiles `d M` and requires
`"5 2"` to match while `"5  2"` does not. `TestTheSeparatorRuleHasOneWriter`
scans the package's non-test sources and requires the inline expression
`tokSpace && mail.Runes(tks[i].text) == 1` to appear only in `tokens.go`.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `space` accepting any white-space run
(`space("5  2", 1) = 2, want 1` and `a two-space run was accepted as the single
separator`); `pattern.go` re-spelling the check
(`the one-character space rule is written in [pattern.go tokens.go]`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/locale`; `go test ./internal/locale` passes;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Environment note.** The first gate run after this edit failed with `no space
left on device` (the host had 18 MB free, shared `/tmp` holds other work).
`go clean -cache` reclaimed the 20 GB regenerable Go build cache and the rerun
was fully green; no source or test changed in between.

**Residual risk.** The rule now covers the two matchers that shared it; a third
token matcher must call `space` rather than compare the token by hand, which the
source guard enforces. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One catalog lookup and one cpu fact for the sidecar

The secrets/fsx/sidecar/locale audit's two sidecar mediums: the "resolve a
runtime and its platform" lookup was written four times, and "does this platform
have a cpu build" had no owner.

**One lookup.** `Catalog.platformOf(runtime, platform)` (in `spec.go`, beside
`Resolve`) returns the runtime, its platform, and the one typed
`ErrUnsupported` answer: an unknown runtime and a runtime without builds for
this machine. It is used by:

- `Resolve` (was an unchecked platform read plus its own unknown-runtime wrap);
- `DefaultBuild` (its own two wraps);
- `probeAuto` (its own "has no builds for" wrap);
- `choiceKey`, which previously **silently proceeded on a zero `Platform`**
  (a zero auto list and no cpu, so a wrong key) and now returns the typed
  error.

**One cpu fact.** `Platform.hasCPU()` owns "this platform ships a cpu build",
with a value receiver so it is callable on a platform read out of the catalog
map. It replaces the four hand-written map checks plus the two inside
`Platform` itself:

- `start.go`'s `instance.hasCPU(b Build)` delegates to it;
- `canary.go`'s reference-builder check uses it;
- `auto.go`'s candidate list and cpu-less probe branch use it;
- `spec.go`'s validation rule (`auto` with no GPU list requires cpu) and
  `defaultVariant` use it.

**Regressions.** `TestPlatformOfIsOneUnsupportedClassification` drives an
unknown runtime and a platform without builds through `platformOf`, `Resolve`
and `DefaultBuild` and requires the **verbatim** same `ErrUnsupported` text from
all three, then checks the supported pair. `TestPlatformHasCPUIsTheOneFact`
pins the shipped catalog (linux has cpu, windows does not), the default variant
that follows it, and the validation rule that reads it.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the shared message drifting (`… has no
build for plan9/386`); `DefaultBuild` re-implementing the lookup with its own
wording (`unknown runtime: nope`); the cpu fact inverted (the validation rule
reports `a cpu variant is required` for linux).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/sidecar`; `go test ./internal/sidecar` passes
(29.4 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs,
87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `Resolve` with an unknown *platform* now answers "runtime X
has no builds for Y" instead of its previous "runtime X has no <variant> build
for Y (it has [])"; the new text is the shared classification and no test or
client reads the old one. `choiceKey` can now return an unsupported-catalog
error where it used to build a key from zero values; the catalog is validated at
load, so that path is defensive. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One classification for a store write that ends an index run

The config/index/syncer/learning audit's fourth medium: `ConfirmEmbeddings` and
`SaveEmbeddings` each classified a failed store write themselves. Both checked
`errors.Is(err, ErrStoreBusy)` and then `ctx.Err()`, but returned differently:
the confirm path returned the store error on cancellation while the save path
returned the context error, so the same event surfaced as two different run
errors.

`index.storeStop(ctx, err, rep) (ret error, handled bool)` now owns the
classification, next to `fail` (the other run-stop owner): a busy store marks
`StoppedBusy` and ends the run with `nil` (the vectors stay uncommitted and the
same mail is embedded next run), an ended context marks `StoppedCancelled` and
returns `context.Cause(ctx)`, and anything else is the caller's own error (each
keeps its wording, e.g. `index: cannot store N vector(s)`). Both call sites are
now three lines.

**Regressions.** `TestStoreStopIsOneClassification` covers the three outcomes,
requires the busy stop to carry the store's message, the cancelled stop to
return the cause (including a `CancelCause` cause), the real failure to be
unhandled, and `Report.Committed()` to stay false in every stopped case. The
existing behaviour tests still pass unchanged, including
`TestStoreBusyExhaustionStopsWithoutQuarantining` (nothing stored or
quarantined, the next run indexes the mail) and the cancelled-retry test.

Mutations, each failing as intended: the busy stop dropping `rep.Error`
(`the stop does not carry the store's message`); cancellation returning the
surface error (`returned write refused, want context canceled`); the busy branch
disabled (the unit table *and* the existing exhaustion test fail).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/index`; `go test ./internal/index` passes
(11.3 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs,
87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The cancelled confirm path now returns the context cause
instead of the store's error; `outcome` already preferred the cause for a
cancelled run, and the error text is not a contract. The deployed build
predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One name per index setting and one role fingerprint

The config/index/syncer/learning audit's fifth medium, plus the settings drift
it sat next to. `internal/index` read six schema keys as literals
(`index.folder_roles`, `index.retry_unavailable`, `index.max_logged_failures`,
`index.runs.keep`, `index.after_sync`, and the existing
`index.quarantine_after`), and the covered-folder-role fingerprint was spelled
twice: `rolesKey(scopeOf(...))` for the coverage key and
`strings.Join(s.Strings("index.folder_roles"), "\x00")` in `retryKeyFor`.

- `internal/index/settings.go` now declares all six names, with the doc comment
  `index/settings.go` already established. Every read site uses one.
- `retryKeyFor` derives its roles through `scopeOf` + `rolesKey`, so the retry
  key and the coverage key share one fingerprint. The audit's failure mode (a
  second spelling drifting and silently re-arming a wait for a scope that no
  longer exists) is gone.
- `rolesKey` is now canonical: it sorts and compacts before joining. Reordering
  `index.folder_roles` (or repeating a role) is the same coverage, so it no
  longer causes a needless cache miss and re-plan, and two different sets still
  cannot collide because a role cannot contain NUL.

**Regressions.** `TestSettingConstantsResolve` requires each constant in
`config.Embedded()` with the type its reader uses;
`TestEverySettingConstantIsListed` scans `settings.go` and requires the schema
table to cover every declaration; `TestNoSettingKeyLiteralAtReadSites` scans the
package's non-test sources for `.Int/Bool/Duration/Float/String(/Strings)`
followed by an `index.` literal.
`TestRetryKeySharesTheCoverageRoleFingerprint` sets the roles out of
alphabetical order and requires the retry key to equal
`rolesKey(scopeOf(snapshot))`, then changes the setting and requires the key to
change. `TestRolesKeyIsCanonical` pins order-insensitivity, duplicate
insensitivity and non-collision (including `["inbox","sent"]` vs
`["inboxsent"]`).

Mutations, each failing as intended: `retryKeyFor` re-spelling the join
(`retry roles "sent\x00inbox", coverage roles "inbox\x00sent"`); `rolesKey`
keeping the config order (`[inbox sent] and [sent inbox] fingerprint
differently`); the separator disappearing (`[inbox sent] and [inboxsent]
collide`); a drifted constant (`"index.folder_role" is not a schema setting`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/index`; `go test ./internal/index` passes
(9.3 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs,
87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The canonical fingerprint makes reordering a no-op, so a
future consumer that cared about the configured order must not read
`rolesKey`; the coverage query still uses the configured slice. The
`store`-owned `index.store_busy_*` keys are read only in the store and stay
named there. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One name per sync setting

The config/index/syncer/learning audit's sixth medium: the `sync.*` keys were
spelled at every read site, so the same key had two or three owners and a typo
would silently read the schema default. `sync.batch_size` was read in
`folder.go`, `scope.go` and `store/fts.go` (twice); `sync.max_logged_skips` in
three files; `sync.details.batch_size` in two; `sync.removal.auto_apply_after`
in `removal.go` and `cmd/mailsense/apiwire.go`; the detail-pass keys in
`livetest` too.

All of them are now named once, following the `index/settings.go` and
`triage` pattern:

- `internal/syncer/settings.go` declares 18 `Setting*` constants for the
  `sync.*`, `contacts.sync.*` and `calendar.sync.*` keys the package reads,
  with a comment on each.
- `sync.batch_size` is owned by the **store**, which sizes the write batch:
  `store.SettingSyncBatchSize` in `internal/store/settings.go`, re-exported as
  `syncer.SettingBatchSize` (the same shape `triage` uses for
  `store.SettingTriageFolderRoles`). This also avoids the import cycle the
  syncer-side constant would have created for `store/fts.go`.
- Every read site uses a constant: `backfill.go`, `details.go`, `discover.go`,
  `folder.go`, `removal.go`, `scheduler.go`, `scope.go`, `world.go`,
  `store/fts.go`, `cmd/mailsense/apiwire.go` and `internal/livetest`.

**Regressions.** `TestSettingConstantsResolve` requires every constant to exist
in `config.Embedded()` **with the type its reader uses**, and that the syncer
and the store agree on the batch-size key.
`TestEverySettingConstantIsListed` reads `settings.go`, counts its declarations
and requires the schema table to cover exactly that set, so a constant added
later cannot skip the check. `TestNoSettingKeyLiteralAtReadSites` scans the
package's non-test sources and fails on any
`.Int/Bool/Duration/Float/String("sync.…")` literal, so the defect cannot be
re-introduced quietly.

Mutations, each failing as intended: a drifted constant
(`"sync.details.batchsize" is not a schema setting`); one read site spelling the
key again (`folder.go reads the key literal .Int("sync.batch_size"; use its
Setting* constant`); an extra constant the table does not check (`settings.go
declares 19 constants, the schema table checks 18`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/syncer ./internal/store ./internal/livetest
./cmd/mailsense`; `go test ./internal/syncer ./internal/store
./cmd/mailsense` passes (store 30 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast
checks passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The schema check pins keys and types, not the accessor each
reader calls; a reader switching `Int` to `Bool` on an int key still panics at
runtime, and no test in the package exercises every accessor. `livetest` is
test support and now depends on `syncer` for the two detail-pass names. The
deployed build predates this change.

The api/cmd audit's remaining error findings: three of the wire's most common

## 2026-11-04 — De-flaking the picked-sync start assertion

The new gate run failed one package, `internal/syncer`:

```
--- FAIL: TestStartPickedSyncsPickedMailboxesAndRecordsTheOwner
    startpicked_test.go:63: jobs after pick: [{... Kind:sync Name:fake Status:succeeded ...}]
```

The test started a picked sync and immediately required the job manager's list
to report `runstate.Running`. The job runs on its own goroutine, so a fast run
(here 2 ms) could finish before that read: the assertion measured the scheduler,
not the start. It passed 300 isolated runs before and after, and reproduced only
inside the loaded 58-package shard.

The assertion now checks what the start actually guarantees — exactly one job,
of the sync kind, named for the source — and leaves the outcome to the existing
`waitJob` (succeeded), owner-identity and per-role count checks. The comment
records why "running right now" is not part of the contract.

**Proof of the mechanism.** Applying the removed assertion **after** the job has
finished fails deterministically with `the old running assertion sees succeeded`;
the new assertion holds in the same position. Nothing else about the test
changed, and the sync code is untouched.

**Evidence.** `go test ./internal/syncer -run TestStartPicked -count=20` passes;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`) on the fixed tree.

**Residual risk.** A test that wants to observe a job mid-flight must block its
body (as `jobs`' own lifecycle tests do with a channel); asserting a live status
after an unblocked start is a race by construction. The deployed build predates
this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One empty-array rule for every API list

The api/cmd audit's third medium: the "a list is `[]`, never `null`" invariant
was written by hand at every endpoint. Three type-specific helpers
(`nonNilStrings`, `nonNilLearned`, `nonNilMailboxes`) and **24 inlined guards**
(`if x == nil { x = []T{} }`) meant a new endpoint could forget the rule, and
each spelling was invisible to the others.

`internal/api/wire.go` now owns it:

```go
func nonNilSlice[T any](s []T) []T            // nil []T -> []T{} ([] on the wire)
func nonNilMap[M ~map[K]V, K comparable, V any](m M) M // nil map -> {} on the wire
```

Every site calls it: ask history, boot views, brief section items **and** their
nested evidence, commitments items/counts, held folders, jobs, log entries, the
all-mail list, providers/providers roles/discovered models, questions, sidecar
builds/runtimes, secret names/expected, settings/restart-pending, status
sources/restart-pending/store-meta, thread messages/participants, mailbox lists,
and `WireMessage`'s attachments. The three helpers are deleted; no hand-written
`== nil` array or object guard remains in the package.

**Regression.** `TestListEndpointsNeverAnswerNull` drives all 17 list-bearing
endpoints against a world whose services return **nothing at all** (nil slices
and maps; `nilListSettings`/`emptyLogs` stubs for the two fakes that used to
return non-nil empty slices, so the handler's rule is what is measured) and
requires every list field to decode as an array and every object field as an
object, never `null`. `TestWireMessageAlwaysCarriesAnAttachmentsArray` covers the
one projection that owns an array outside a handler.

Mutations, each failing as intended: `nonNilSlice` returning its input
(`[items] = <nil>, want an array (null is not a list)`, then every other list);
deleting the jobs endpoint's call (`[jobs] = <nil>, …`); `nonNilMap` returning
its input (`[counts] = <nil>, want an object (null is not an empty object)` and
`[store_meta]`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/api`; `go test ./internal/api` and
`go test -race ./internal/api` (7 s) pass; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all
fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The rule covers the lists the handlers own; a service that
marshals its own nested response still owns its arrays (the brief sections and
`WireMessage` are the two in-package projections, and both are covered). A nil
element inside a list is still `null`, deliberately: "no rows" and "a null row"
are different facts. The deployed build predates this change.

packages; three sites had their own copy:

- `config/layers.go readFileLayer` (settings.json);
- `config/learned.go readLearnedLayer` (install-profile.json) and
  `readProfileDoc` (the same file, on the edit path);
- `secrets/filestore.go openFileStore` (the sealed secret file).

All four now call `fsx.ReadOptional(path)` and branch on its `(data, ok, err)`:
absent is the empty layer / empty document / empty writable store, any other
failure is reported at the same place as before (`problems.add` for config, the
returned error for the secret store and the edit path). `config/layers.go` lost
`errors`, `io/fs` and `os`; `config/learned.go` lost the same three;
`secrets/filestore.go` lost `io/fs` and `os`.

**Regressions.** `TestUnreadableConfigFilesStayProblems` puts a **directory** at
each optional config path (a failure that is not "absent") and requires a
problem naming that path, then confirms an absent pair still loads at the
default layer. `TestProfileDocWithUnreadableFile` requires the edit path to
return the failure instead of editing an empty document it could not read.
`TestFileStoreOptionalFile` requires an absent secret file to open as a writable
empty store and a directory at that path to be an error.

Mutation check: making `fsx.ReadOptional` swallow every read failure as absent
fails all three with `a directory at …/settings.json was treated as an absent
file`, `a directory at the install profile was read as a missing document` and
`a directory at the secret path opened as an empty store`.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/config ./internal/secrets ./internal/fsx`;
`go test ./internal/config ./internal/secrets ./internal/fsx` passes;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** Each caller still decides what an absent file means (an empty
layer, an empty document, a new store); `fsx.ReadOptional` owns only the read.
The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One order and one cap for a company's open threads

The api/cmd and config/index/syncer/learning audits left this one behind, and an
independent repo-wide block scan confirmed it as the only remaining exact
cross-package duplicate outside the audited scopes: the ordering of a company's
open threads plus the display cap lived twice.

`internal/store/companyprofile.go` and `internal/world/world.go` each spelled the
same comparator (state order, then `LastAt` newest first, then
`ConversationID` as the stable tie-break) and then applied the same
`store.CompanyProfileOpenCap` (20). Both packages present the same list (the
profile route and the hub's company projection), so a change to one could drift
the other by a tie-break or an uncapped list, and no test could see it: each
copy was correct on its own.

`store.OrderCompanyThreads(open []CompanyThread) []CompanyThread` is now the one
owner, next to the type and the cap. It sorts in place and returns the capped
slice; `companyOpenThreadsFrom` returns `OrderCompanyThreads(open), counts` and
`world` returns `counts, store.OrderCompanyThreads(open)`. `world` no longer
imports `sort`.

**Regressions.** `TestOrderCompanyThreadsIsTheListContract` pins all four facts
at once: state order across five real states plus an unknown state string, newest
first inside a state, the conversation-id tie-break for equal timestamps, and the
cap (27 threads in, 20 out, the first 20 of the ordered list); it also requires
a nil list to stay empty. `TestCompanyThreadOrderHasOneOwner` scans the non-test
sources of `internal/store` and `internal/world` and requires the ordering to
appear in `companyprofile.go` only, the cap to appear in `companyprofile.go`
only, and `world.go` to delegate through `store.OrderCompanyThreads(open)`.

Mutations, each failing as intended: reversing the conversation-id tie-break
(`order [c-owner-tie a-owner-new …], want [a-owner-new c-owner-tie …]`); removing
the cap (`27 threads after the cap, want 20`); re-spelling the sort and the cap
in `world` (`../world/world.go applies the open-thread cap outside
companyprofile.go`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/store ./internal/world`; `go test
./internal/store ./internal/world` passes (store 29.7 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh`
reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar,
`-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `OrderCompanyThreads` sorts its caller's slice in place, as
both call sites already did, and the scan guards only the two packages shown
here; a third producer of `CompanyThread` would need its own call, which the
type's doc should make obvious. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One gate reading for Open, Allow and PreviewAnswers

The config/index/syncer/learning audit's medium finding in `internal/learning`:
the gate state was derived twice. `GateState` existed as the documented "one
consistent reading" (its own comment says asking the three questions separately
"can produce a view that never existed"), yet the three questioned answered
themselves:

- `Open` re-derived `(open, err)` from the raw rule error;
- `Allow` re-derived the lock-vs-failure split (with its deliberate
  no-gate-read shortcut while the test preview is on);
- `PreviewAnswers` called `Open` and then re-applied its own `err == nil &&
  !open` rule.

The two derivations disagreed on a broken rule: `PreviewAnswers` refused the
preview (`err == nil` fails) while `GateState.Preview` was `!open`, so the
`/api/gate` route (the only `GateState` consumer) could report `preview: true`
for a failed latch that `PreviewAnswers` had already refused. This round removes
the second derivation instead of reconciling it:

- `Open` returns `GateState(ctx).Open` and `.Err`;
- `PreviewAnswers` returns `GateState(ctx).Preview`;
- `Allow` keeps its one documented shortcut (preview on means allowed without
  reading the rule at all, so a broken latch cannot block a screen the preview
  exists to unblock) and otherwise returns `GateState(ctx).Allow`;
- `GateState.Preview` is `previewing && !open && raw == nil`, so a broken rule
  is not a closed gate, and its field comments now say so.

The lock-vs-failure split and the "preview hides the lock but never a broken
latch or status read" rule therefore exist once, in `GateState`.

**Regressions.** `TestGateStateIsOneConsistentReading` now, for each of its four
cases (setting off/on × gate closed/open), also requires `Open`,
`PreviewAnswers` and `Allow` to answer exactly what `GateState` answered, and
pins the shortcut: `Allow` reads the learned scope **zero** times while the
preview is on and once otherwise. `TestGateStateKeepsTheRawFailureUnderThePreview`
now requires `Preview` to stay false on a broken latch, `PreviewAnswers` to
agree, `Open` to return the failure and `Allow` to depend only on the setting.

Mutation checks: `preview = !open` (the old second rule) fails with `a failed
rule claimed the test preview`; removing `Allow`'s shortcut fails with `Allow
read the rule 1 times, want 0 (preview=true)`.

**Evidence.** `go vet` for learning, api, triage, qa, priority, search, brief
and conversations; `go test ./internal/learning ./internal/api
./internal/triage` passes; `go test -race ./internal/learning` passes (12.9 s);
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `PreviewAnswers` now reads the rule through `GateState`,
which also builds the allowance; the extra work is the same single latch read,
and the alternative (deriving `Preview` from `Open` again) is what this round
removes. The API's `fakeLearning` stub still sets `preview`/`open`/`allowErr`
independently, which is a test double, not a second owner. The deployed build
predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One bounded join for the API handlers and the sidecar supervisors

First audit pass over the packages no earlier round owned (`internal/api`,
`cmd/mailsense`, `internal/config`, `internal/index`, `internal/syncer`,
`internal/learning`, `internal/secrets`, `internal/fsx`, `internal/sidecar`,
`internal/locale`). It found two **highs**, and they are the same defect in two
packages: a service re-implementing `join.Group`'s bounded join.

- `internal/api/server.go` kept `handlersClosed` + `handlersActive` +
  `sync.WaitGroup` + `enterHandler`/`leaveHandler`/`joinHandlers` under one
  mutex: Track, Done and Close with a bound, minus the owner.
- `internal/sidecar/manager.go` kept `stopped` + `workers` + `sync.WaitGroup`
  under one mutex: the same gate and the same bounded wait for supervisors.

Both now hold a `join.Group`. The owner gained the two verbs the callers
actually needed, both documented beside the existing ones:

- `Refuse()` closes the admission gate **without waiting**. `Shutdown` must
  refuse new handlers before it drains the listener and join afterwards;
  expressing that with `Close` would have waited before shutting the server
  down. `Close` is now `Refuse` + wait, so there is still one closed flag.
- `Active()` is the count the shutdown log reports (`left=N`) and the API's
  `ErrHandlersUnjoined` message names. It is a read of the join state, not a
  scheduling signal.

Behaviour preserved: `enterHandler` → `Track` (false → 503), `leaveHandler` →
`Done`, `joinHandlers` → `Close(ctx)` and an unjoined error only for a handler
still active after the bound; `startWorker` → `Track`, `Stop` → cancel +
`Close(ctx)` bounded by `sidecar.stop_timeout + supervisorJoinSlack`. The
sidecar pool now owns the one `Done` (removed from `supervise`), so a supervisor
that returns or panics always retires its slot.

**Regressions.** The invariants that existed before the change pass unchanged:
`TestStartWorkerIsSerializedWithStop` (a racing start either joins and is waited
for or is refused; no supervisor starts after `Stop`), `TestStopIsBoundedWhenAWorkerNeverFinishes`
(the bounded wait, the `left=1` warning and the give-up point), the API's
unjoined-handler test (`ErrHandlersUnjoined` wrapping the expired context) and
its `shutting_down` 503 tests. New `TestRefuseClosesTheGateWithoutWaiting` pins
the split: refuse closes the gate and leaves the task counted, a later `Close`
joins it.

Mutation checks: an API `enterHandler` that admits unconditionally fails with
`status 200, want 503` and `Shutdown returned context deadline exceeded, want
ErrHandlersUnjoined`; a `Stop` that refuses without joining fails with `Stop
returned before its workers were released`.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/join ./internal/api ./internal/sidecar`; `go
test` for the three (sidecar 31 s); `go test -race ./internal/join
./internal/api` (7 s) and `-race ./internal/sidecar` (50 s); `scripts/test-fast.sh`
reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar,
`-race qa+api`); `scripts/test-ui.sh runtime.spec.ts boot.spec.ts` 18 passed,
covering the real server's start/stop path.

**Residual risk.** A second concurrent `Stop`/`Shutdown` now waits on the same
drain (bounded) instead of returning at once; `join.Close` documents that, and
the app calls each once. The audits' remaining findings are medium/low and are
the next rounds: the `ErrSourceBusy` wrap built three times, `learning.GateState`
re-derived by `Open`/`Allow`/`PreviewAnswers`, three optional-file reads that
should call `fsx.ReadOptional`, the index store-stop classification, the folder
role fingerprint, `sync.*` keys spelled at their read sites, the API's
`nonNilSlice[T]`/`not_found`/`shutting_down` repetitions, the `apiwire`
sentinel re-declarations, and the sidecar catalog lookup built four times. The
deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — De-flaking the two rotating e2e failures

The last open report item: a full `scripts/test-ui.sh` run kept failing one
unrelated spec under load (the boot scroll restore once, the learning
certification gate another time), each passing alone.

**Reproduction.** None on this tree. Three full runs at `--workers=4` while
eight CPU burners held the host at load average 46 (12 cores) passed 179/179
(1.4 m, 1.4 m, 1.2 m), and twenty repeats of each suspect spec at three workers
under the same load passed 20/20 each. The earlier failures therefore predate
the router focus/refresh round (which stopped a live refresh replacing the
mounted screen and stopped mounts stealing focus from the shell search bar) and
no longer reproduce here; this round hardens the two waits that could produce
that exact signature instead of claiming a cause it cannot observe.

**What could still produce "one unrelated spec fails, passes alone":**

- `learning.spec.ts` waited on an **unbounded** promise for the app's
  `/api/hub` read. A boot that never asked for the snapshot left the test to
  the 45 s Playwright timeout, which is reported as an unrelated stalled spec.
  It now polls a flag with the assertion budget and a named message.
- `boot.spec.ts`'s DOM-cache test read the restored scroll **once**, right after
  `expectRoute`, which by the boot contract names the *skeleton* mount, not the
  painted screen. The read is now null-safe and polls the restored position;
  a screen that was rebuilt instead of restored still fails, because the
  injected filler does not exist in a fresh node.

A third hypothesis was tested and rejected before landing: giving `app.goto` a
30 s boot budget and waiting for `data-screen`. The boot-contract test proves
the router paints its skeleton *before* the status, gate and language reads, so
the attribute cannot stand for "boot finished"; the change (and a slow-boot
spec built on it) was reverted, not shipped.

**One owner for the route attribute.** `data-screen` had two writers: the
router's `setHeader` and the language pass, which re-spelled it from
`state.route` and could name a route the router had not mounted (and, with no
token, one it never would). The language write is gone; `TestRouteAttributeHasOneWriter`
reads every JS module and requires exactly one writer, inside `setHeader`.

**Mutation checks.** A second `dataset.screen` writer in `10-language.js` fails
with `route attribute writers [10-language.js 12-router.js]`. A restore that
skips `[data-scroll-key]` nodes fails the boot spec with `the cached route did
not restore its section scroll`. An app that never reads `/api/hub` (both the
prefetch and the learning render removed) fails the learning spec in ~8 s with
`the app never read /api/hub` instead of stalling to 45 s.

**Evidence.** `scripts/test-ui.sh --workers=4` twice: 179 passed (1.4 m, 1.2 m),
both with the eight burners still active; `scripts/test-ui.sh boot.spec.ts
learning.spec.ts`: 25 passed; `go test ./internal/ui` including
`TestGeneratedBundlesAreCurrent` and the new guard; `scripts/test-fast.sh`
reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar,
`-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The original intermittent failure was never reproduced, so
this round cannot claim to have found its root cause; what it can claim is that
the two rotating specs no longer depend on an unbounded wait or a one-shot
read. `data-screen` still names the skeleton mount by design, so a test that
needs painted content must wait for that content (auto-retrying assertions or
the new polls), not for the route. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One context-aware map-reduce for the evidence workers

The judge/feedback/evidence/threads audit's last medium: the engine had three
hand-rolled worker pools. Two are now one helper; the third stays, with its
reason written down.

**One pool.** `evidence.mapReduce[T, R](ctx, workers, items, label, fn, merge)`
in `internal/evidence/parallel.go` is the one pool: it offers every item to at
most `workers` goroutines, guards each call with `safely` (a panic becomes that
item's error, logged once), merges each successful result under one mutex, and
returns only after every worker exited. A cancelled context stops the producer
and skips the items already handed off; the cancellation is not reported as an
item error, so the caller can tell a cancelled run from a broken message. The
first failure is the lowest item index, so two broken messages always report the
same one.

- `run.go`'s batch pool is now one `mapReduce` call over the batch's rows: its
  per-index `out`/`computed` arrays are written by the merge closure, and the
  caller keeps the one "the cause wins over an interrupted item's error"
  ordering before it inspects the batch.
- `templates.go`'s sender groups are now the same pool, and `buildTemplates`
  takes a `context.Context` for the first time: the template pass covers every
  message with a vector, so shutdown used to wait for it to finish the whole
  mailbox. It now abandons the rest and returns the cause.
- `passone.go` keeps its own streaming loop, with a comment saying why: the
  store cursor is the producer, so only a bounded window of rows is resident;
  `mapReduce` works from a materialized slice, which there would hold the whole
  mailbox in memory. Same shape, different memory contract.

**Regressions.** `TestMapReduceMergesEveryItemOnce` runs 500 items on 1, 2 and 8
workers and requires every result at its own index; `TestMapReduceTurnsAPanicIntoThatItemsError`
panics in two items, requires a `jobs.PanicError` naming the **lower** one, and
requires the other 38 items to run and merge; `TestMapReduceStopsTheProducerOnCancellation`
cancels inside the first of 100,000 items and requires exactly one start and a
prompt return; `TestMapReduceLeavesNoWorkerBehind` checks the goroutine count
after five runs; `TestBuildTemplatesStopsOnCancellation` pre-cancels a 100-sender
pass and requires the cause and no counts.

Mutation checks: dropping `safely` crashes the binary (`panic: synthetic
evidence worker crash`); returning the last error fails the deterministic-first
assertion; deleting the cancelled-`buildTemplates` check fails with `error
<nil>, want the cancellation cause`; removing both cancellation paths from the
pool fails with `100000 items started after the first cancelled; want 1`. The
worker-side skip alone is not observable on its own: the unbuffered handoff and
the producer's stop already bound it to the items in flight, so it stays as
defence in depth and is not claimed as the guarantee. At the run level the
existing `TestCancelInterruptsAnInFlightBatch` still proves a huge batch is
abandoned and nothing of it is written.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/evidence`; `go test ./internal/evidence
-count=1` (16.7 s) and `go test -race ./internal/evidence -count=1` (52 s) pass;
`scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87
packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The pool's `merge` runs on a worker goroutine under one mutex
and is documented as a plain assignment; a merge that panics is not recovered.
`buildTemplates` now returns an error on cancellation, which `buildEnv` surfaces
as a cancelled run, the same contract as the rest of the context build. The
deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One count rule for every Brief section

The last low finding of the hub/brief/world/conversations/search audit. Four
section builders each restated "a section reports at least the rows it shows",
in three different shapes:

- `commitmentSection` trusted `open.Counts[direction]`, which is `0` when the
  map has no entry for that direction;
- `changedSection` raised `facts.RecentTotal` to `len(items)` only when the
  total was exactly zero;
- `relationshipSection` raised the total when it was below the rows;
- `topicSection` reported `census.Classified` raw while raising its own `Total`
  from the census.

`brief.sectionCount(total, shown)` is now the one rule (`max(total, shown)`), the
four builders call it, and an honest total is still never inflated. The
zero-total special case disappeared: `max(0, len(items))` is the same answer.

**Regressions.** `TestEverySectionCountsAtLeastWhatItShows` drives all four
builders twice: once with a source that under-reports (no direction count, no
recent total, no organization total, `Classified: 0` beside one topic) and once
with an honest total that must survive untouched; it also requires a section's
`Total` never to fall below its `Count`. Mutation checks: reporting the raw
direction map fails with `count 0 below the 2 rows shown`; reporting the raw
organization total fails the same way.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/brief`; `go test ./internal/brief
./internal/api` passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed
(9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** The rule protects the wire payload, not a broken source: an
under-reported count now silently equals the visible rows instead of the true
total, which is the honest minimum. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One reply example, one latency rounding and one month key

The judge/feedback/evidence/threads audit's medium reply-projection finding, and
the month key it exposed one package further out.

**One reply example.** `Profile.addExample` and `KnownHistory` each built the
`Example` literal (`MessageID`, `Subject`, `ReceivedAt` in the zone,
`RespondedMinutes`, `ReplyPreview`), so a field added to one surface could miss
the other. `threads.newExample(m, r, zone)` is now the one builder, and the
owner's-zone instant it renders has one helper (`stampIn`), which `Stats`'
`FirstSeen`/`LastSeen` also use. The local offset is deliberate and documented
against `mail.Stamp`'s stored UTC form.

**One latency rounding.** `RoundMinutes` + `MinutePlaces` in `internal/threads`
replace `mathx.Round(x/60, 1)` (behaviour twice, history once) and feedback's
copied `const minutePlaces = 1` "as in threads". `medianGroups` and `median1`
now call `threads.RoundMinutes`, so a reply reports one number on every screen.

`volume.go`'s `StdDev` was borrowing `minutePlaces` for a standard deviation of
monthly **counts** — a different fact that merely shared the value 1. It has its
own documented `volumePlaces` instead of inheriting the latency rule.

**One month bucket key.** Removing feedback's `month[:4], month[5:]` meant
naming the owner of the key, and the format ("2006-01") turned out to be spelled
in three packages: `threads` (volume months), `store/companyprofile.go` (company
activity months, two sites) and `store/mailquery.go` (time-plan month buckets,
two sites). `mail` is the lowest package all of them import, so
`mail.MonthKey(t)` and `mail.SplitMonth(key)` now own it; the six sites call
them and no package slices or formats a month itself.

**Regressions.**
`TestBehaviourAndHistoryReportTheSameExample` compares the two surfaces' example
structs and pins the zone and the rounding; `TestProfileMonthsUseTheOwnerMonthKey`
buckets a late instant into the owner's local month; `TestRoundMinutesIsTheOneLatencyRounding`
pins the half-up edge (1.25 min → 1.3); `TestMonthKeyRoundTrips` (mail) walks
every month at both day boundaries in five zones across the date line and pins
that junk keys split to empty; `TestFeedbackAndThreadsReportTheSameLatency`
compares feedback's median with `Behaviour().Totals.MedianMinutes` for replies of
75 s, 80 s and 5 min (a non-whole-minute median); `TestYearOverYearComparesSharedMonthsOnly`
covers the year grouping for the first time, including the junk key that used to
panic a slicing split.

Mutation checks, all failing as intended: history without the zone
(`the two surfaces disagree`); the volume month bucketed in UTC
(`months map[2026-01:…] do not use the owner key "2025-12"`); feedback rounding
to two places (`disagrees with the single median 1.3`); feedback slicing the
month itself (`panic: slice bounds out of range [:4] with length 0`); a month key
without zero padding (`key "2026-1" splits to ""/""`).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/mail ./internal/threads ./internal/feedback
./internal/store ./internal/api`; `go test` for `./internal/mail`,
`./internal/threads`, `./internal/feedback`, `./internal/store` and
`./internal/api` passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed
(9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `Example.ReceivedAt` stays a zone-local RFC 3339 with offset
(the behaviour view is the owner's local view), unlike the UTC wire stamps of
the other responses; that is the documented contract, not a second owner. The
month key format is now one owner, but each caller still decides which zone the
buckets are in. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One wire timestamp for derived instants

The last low finding of the hub/brief/world/conversations/search audit: the
stored timestamp form was rendered by hand in nine response fields —
`hub.Mailbox`'s three sync stamps, `brief`'s `since` and `generated_at`,
`conversations`' two `generated_at` fields and `world`'s two — each spelling
`t.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)`, and `hub` added a zero check per field.

- **One function.** `mail.Stamp(t)` renders the stored form (UTC, second
  precision, `Z`) or `""` for the zero instant. It is the same layout
  `mail.TimeLayout` reads, so the UI can parse a value back with `mail.Parse`.
  All nine sites call it.
- **The zero rule has one owner too.** `hub`'s three `if !x.IsZero()` guards
  were a second expression of "a missing instant is the empty string"; the
  assignment is now direct, with one comment naming the rule.
- **A structural guard keeps it.** `TestNoPackageFormatsAWireTimestampByHand`
  reads the four response packages and fails if any non-test file formats a
  timestamp itself (`Format(time.RFC3339)` or `Format(mail.TimeLayout)`).
  Parsing an input timestamp is explicitly out of scope: the query bounds
  validate their own argument.

**Regressions.** `TestStampIsTheOneWireInstant` pins the zero instant, an offset
instant rendered in UTC at second precision, and the round-trip through
`mail.Parse`. Mutation checks: formatting one `conversations` field by hand
fails with `../conversations/service.go formats a stamp by hand; call
mail.Stamp`; dropping the zero/UTC rule fails with `zero instant
"0001-01-01T00:00:00Z", want the empty string`.

**Evidence.** `go vet` for the five packages; `go test` for `./internal/mail`,
`./internal/hub`, `./internal/brief`, `./internal/conversations`,
`./internal/world` and `./internal/api` passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports
all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `mail.Stamp` always renders UTC, which is what every current
wire field wants; a future field that must show the owner's local offset needs
its own explicit formatter. The deployed build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One limit rule, one list copier, and no dead world helpers

Three small duplicates and one dead function from the hub/brief/world/
conversations/search audit, all in `internal/world`, `internal/conversations`
and `internal/mathx`.

- **One bounded-limit rule.** `world` had `clampListLimit`, `clampMonths` and
  `clampEventDays` (three copies of "below the floor → default, above the
  maximum → maximum") and `conversations` had a fourth, `clampLimit`. All four
  are `mathx.Clamp(v, fallback, max)`, which now states the shape once; each
  caller keeps its own default and maximum. The four local functions are
  deleted.
- **One non-nil list copier.** `world` had six helpers
  (`copyStrings`, `copyPeople`, `copyMonths`, `copyMessages`,
  `copyCalendarEvents`, `copyDeadlines`) that were character-for-character the
  same body. One generic `nonNil[T]` replaces them, with the reason they exist
  in one comment: every list a profile view sends is an array, never `null`.
- **Dead and empty helpers removed.** `world.stateOrder` had no caller (the
  profile list already sorts by `threadintel.StateOrder`), and
  `companyStateCounts`/`isOpenState` were one-line pass-throughs to
  `threadintel.StateCounts(nil)`/`threadintel.IsOpen`; the call sites now read
  the owner directly.

**Regressions.** `TestClampIsTheOneLimitRule` (mathx) tables negative, zero,
the floor, a valid value, the maximum and the maximum+1.
`TestEveryProfileListIsAnArray` (world) marshals every empty profile list and
requires `[]` (never `null`) and requires `nonNil` to copy rather than alias.
Mutation checks: a `Clamp` floor of 0 fails with `Clamp(0, 25, 200) = 0, want
25`; a `nonNil` that returns its input fails with `messages list marshals as
null, want []` (and the same for events and deadlines).

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/world ./internal/mathx
./internal/conversations`; `go test` for those plus `./internal/store` and
`./internal/api` passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports all fast checks passed
(9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** `mathx.Clamp` assumes the valid floor is 1, which is true
for every current caller (all four minima are 1); a caller needing a different

duration with a different rule and stays separate on purpose. The deployed
build predates this change.

## 2026-11-04 — One ask table for the classifier, the resolver and the ranking

The priority/agenda/commitments/action audit's last high finding: the profile's
`asks_for` vocabulary was re-listed three times. `action.primaryFor` mapped
seven asks to a primary action, `priority.actionAsk` re-typed the five concrete
ones for the ranking's "an explicit ask always enters" rule, and
`threadintel.asksOther` re-typed six for the resolver's "does this ask the other
side for something".

Two facts, two owners, at the lowest package each belongs to:

- **`threadintel`** owns the vocabulary's structural meaning — `Ask`
  (`AskNone`/`AskReply`/`AskWork`/`AskFYI`), `ClassifyAsk(asksFor)` and

  imports `threadintel`), so the classification cannot live above it.
  `Message.asksOther` is now one call to it.
- **`action`** owns the owner-facing consequence —
  `AskAction(asksFor) (Primary, bool)`, where the bool is "concrete work".
  `primaryFor` uses `threadintel.ClassifyAsk` for "is this an ask at all / is it
  an FYI" and `AskAction` for the action and the reason
  (`ask:<option>` or `fyi`), and `priority.actionAsk` is now that table's
  concrete flag.

Behaviour is unchanged: `other`, an empty value and an unknown option are still
`AskNone`, so they fall through to the reply/CTA rules, and the primary actions
and reason strings are byte-identical.

**Regressions.** `TestClassifyAskIsTheOneVocabulary` (threadintel) tables the
eight profile options plus empty, unknown, spacing and case, and asserts the
message method is the same rule. `TestAskActionCoversEveryProfileOption`
(action) walks *every* `asks_for` option of the default profile and requires a
reviewed action, `concrete == (threadintel.ClassifyAsk == AskWork)`, and a
non-concrete answer for an empty value; it also fails when the reviewed table
names an option the profile dropped. `TestClassifierUsesTheAskTable` requires
`primaryFor` to return the table's action and its own reason.
`TestConcreteAskIsTheRankingsEntryRule` (priority) drives every profile option
through `Score` and requires the ranking to enter exactly when the table says
concrete, with the `action` reason.

Mutation checks: `task_work` returning `(Do, false)` fails the action table with
`"task_work" -> "do" concrete=false, want "do" concrete=true`; giving the
ranking its old four-option list fails with `ranking entry false for
"task_work", want true`; a vocabulary typo fails with
`ClassifyAsk("answer_question") = 0, want 1`.

**Evidence.** `go vet ./internal/action ./internal/priority
./internal/threadintel`; `go test` for those three plus `./internal/triage`,
`./internal/store` and `./internal/qa` passes; `scripts/test-fast.sh` reports
all fast checks passed (9 vet configs, 87 packages, sidecar, `-race qa+api`).

**Residual risk.** One observation worth keeping: running six heavy packages in
